Here 𝑴\boldsymbol{M} and 𝑲\boldsymbol{K} may not be as meaningful as the mass and stiffness matrices in the second-order ODEs case. The initial conditions are

𝒖|t=0=𝟎,p|t=0=0.\boldsymbol{u}|_{t=0}=\boldsymbol{0},\;p|_{t=0}=0. (5.72)

The acoustic space is often finite, which means boundary conditions are essential to shape the solutions of acoustic equations. Let Γ(c)∈ℝ3\Gamma^{(c)}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} be the acoustic space’s whole solid boundary, of which Γ1(c),Γ2(c)∈Γ(c)\Gamma_{1}^{(c)},\Gamma_{2}^{(c)}\in\Gamma^{(c)} are the room boundary (grounds, walls, ceilings) and piano soundboard parts respectively, as shown in figure 4. In [11], the walls were assumed rigid, which can produce sound reflection effects but may miss sound absorption effects. This motivates our introduction of vibratory acoustic boundaries to account for various phenomena like reflection, scattering, absorption, diffusion, resonance etc.

5.2 Model for the room

In this section, we delve into the specification of room boundary models, which serve as the cornerstone for the subsequent analysis of solid-air coupling dynamics. For the sake of conciseness, we adopt a simplified representation of the room environment as a shoebox-shaped 3D space accommodating a piano. It is worth noting, however, that this room model remains versatile and can be readily adapted to accommodate irregular room geometries. The room’s boundaries—encompassing floors, walls, and ceilings—play pivotal roles in shaping the acoustic behavior within, acting as both reflectors and absorbers of sound waves. In the context of physical modeling, these boundaries are treated as 3D elastic materials, akin to the piano’s soundboard model. This methodological alignment facilitates the straight application of the general 3D elasticity model and the soundboard model to the room, obviating the need for reformulations of the governing equations and weak forms.

The primary specialization within this framework lies in the stipulation of boundary conditions of room barriers. As highlighted red in figure 4, the inner side of ground, wall and ceiling (blue color), defined as Γ1(f)\Gamma_{1}^{(f)}, is the room material’s interface with the air; the underside of ground material (red color), defined as Γ2(f)\Gamma_{2}^{(f)}, is where the Dirichlet boundary condition applies. Firmly rooted in the earth, the ground material should experience zero displacement along Γ2(f)\Gamma_{2}^{(f)}. This condition is written as

𝒖(f)|𝒙∈Γ2(f)=𝟎.\boldsymbol{u}^{(f)}|_{\boldsymbol{x}\in\Gamma_{2}^{(f)}}=\boldsymbol{0}. (5.73)

In case the inner concrete layers of walls and ceilings are considered rigid, displacements on the surfaces of them should be zero too. Another specialization is that prestress need not be considered for room barriers. Even if it exists, the dynamic deformation may not be large enough to induce significant effect of prestress on vibration.

6 Model for coupling between different parts of the piano

6.1 Model for hammer-string coupling

The piano hammer positioned below the string functions the excitation of string vibration, which is known to be a highly nonlinear process [17]. We consider two main parts of the hammer relevant to this excitation process: the wooden hammer shank that can be approximated as non-deformable; the hammer felt that is deformable, impacting and exerting force on the string. Normally, the hammer moves in a circle when triggered by piano player’s key action, striking the string at certain point in during a very short period of time, and is also pushed back by the vibrating string.

6.1.1 One hammer striking one string

For the case of one hammer striking one string, the study follows the 0D nonlinear hammer-string interaction model in [11], with some refinements: for the case of one hammer striking one string, the rotational movement of hammer [12] and the horizontal interaction force are taken into account.

As shown in figure 5, x​y​zxyz is the coordinate system of piano string, where the xx axis of the string system has an angle α0\alpha_{0} to the ground. To better describe the hammer shank motion which is rotation around point P1P_{1}, we will not often the use the x​y​zxyz system. Instead, we define a static coordinate system x′​y′​z′x^{\prime}y^{\prime}z^{\prime} with origin P1P_{1}, y′y^{\prime} axis the same as yy axis, z′z^{\prime} axis with negative direction the same as gravity, and x′x^{\prime} axis perpendicular to the y′​O′​z′y^{\prime}O^{\prime}z^{\prime} plane. The motion of hammer shank as a rigid body can then be described as rotating around the y′y^{\prime} axis and not moving in the y′y^{\prime} direction. We can thus use a single variable θ⁡(t)\theta(t), the angle of P1​P3→\overrightarrow{P_{1}P_{3}} to the x′x^{\prime} axis, to fuuly describe the hammer shank motion. The hammer shank drives the overall motion of the shank head P2P_{2} and felt head P4P_{4}. Nevertheless, when the felt head is in contact with the string’s Q0Q_{0} point, it undergoes a compression ϑ=[ϑ1,ϑ2,ϑ3]⊤\boldsymbol{\vartheta}=[\vartheta_{1},\vartheta_{2},\vartheta_{3}]^{\top} from P4P_{4} to P6P_{6}, which also overlaps with the dynamic string point Q1Q_{1}, which also contributes to its motion. To perform a reasonable orthogonal decomposition of this compression, we define a dynamic coordinate system x′′​y′′​z′′x^{\prime\prime}y^{\prime\prime}z^{\prime\prime} with origin P3P_{3}, x′′x^{\prime\prime} axis with positive direction P5​Q0→\overrightarrow{P_{5}Q_{0}}, y′′y^{\prime\prime} axis with positive direction the same as yy axis, and z′′z^{\prime\prime} axis with positive direction P5​P2→\overrightarrow{P_{5}P_{2}}. The hammer compression can then be decomposed onto the x′′,y′′,z′′x^{\prime\prime},y^{\prime\prime},z^{\prime\prime} axes as marked as marked ϑ1,ϑ2,ϑ3\vartheta_{1},\vartheta_{2},\vartheta_{3} respectively in figure 5.

Denote the displacement of string point Q0Q_{0} with coordinate 𝒙0(a)\boldsymbol{x}_{0}^{(a)} in the x​y​zxyz system as 𝒖0(a)=𝒖(a)​(𝒙0(a),t)\boldsymbol{u}_{0}^{(a)}=\boldsymbol{u}^{(a)}(\boldsymbol{x}_{0}^{(a)},t). Denote the lengths of Q0​P1Q_{0}P_{1}, P0​P1P_{0}P_{1}, P1​P3P_{1}P_{3}, P2​P3P_{2}P_{3}, P1​P2P_{1}P_{2}, P2​P4P_{2}P_{4} as LL, L0L_{0}, L1L_{1}, L2L_{2}, L3L_{3}, L4L_{4} respectively, and the angle of P1​Q0→\overrightarrow{P_{1}Q_{0}} to the x′x^{\prime} axis as α1\alpha_{1}. Our geometric analysis finds the coordinates of Q1Q_{1} (equivalent to P6P_{6} in case of compression) in the x′​y′​z′x^{\prime}y^{\prime}z^{\prime} system and x′′​y′′​z′′x^{\prime\prime}y^{\prime\prime}z^{\prime\prime} system, denoted 𝒙1(a′)\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(a^{\prime})} and 𝒙1(a′′)\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(a^{\prime\prime})}, are

𝒙1(a′)=𝒓0+𝑹0​𝒖0(a),𝒙1(a′′)=𝒓+𝑹⁡(θ)​𝒙1(a′),\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(a^{\prime})}=\boldsymbol{r}_{0}+\boldsymbol{R}_{0}\boldsymbol{u}_{0}^{(a)},\;\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(a^{\prime\prime})}=\boldsymbol{r}+\boldsymbol{R}(\theta)\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(a^{\prime})},
𝒓0=[Lcosα10Lsinα1],𝑹0=[cos⁡α00−sin⁡α0010sin⁡α00cos⁡α0],\displaystyle\boldsymbol{r}_{0}=\left[\begin{array}[]{c}L\cos\alpha_{1}\\ 0\\ L\sin\alpha_{1}\end{array}\right],\;\boldsymbol{R}_{0}=\left[\begin{array}[]{ccc}\cos\alpha_{0}&0&-\sin\alpha_{0}\\ 0&1&0\\ \sin\alpha_{0}&0&\cos\alpha_{0}\end{array}\right],
𝒓=[−L10−L2],𝑹⁡(θ)=[cos⁡θ0sin⁡θ010−sin⁡θ0cos⁡θ].\displaystyle\boldsymbol{r}=\left[\begin{array}[]{c}-L_{1}\\ 0\\ -L_{2}\end{array}\right],\;\boldsymbol{R}(\theta)=\left[\begin{array}[]{ccc}\cos\theta&0&\sin\theta\\ 0&1&0\\ -\sin\theta&0&\cos\theta\end{array}\right].

And converting 𝒙1(a′′)\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(a^{\prime\prime})} to 𝒙1(a′)\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(a^{\prime})} results in

𝒙1(a′)=𝒔⁡(θ)+𝑺⁡(θ)​𝒙1(a′′),\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(a^{\prime})}=\boldsymbol{s}(\theta)+\boldsymbol{S}(\theta)\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(a^{\prime\prime})},
𝒔⁡(θ)=[L1​cos⁡θ−L2​sin⁡θ0L1​sin⁡θ+L2​cos⁡θ],𝑺⁡(θ)=[cos⁡θ0−sin⁡θ010sin⁡θ0cos⁡θ].\displaystyle\boldsymbol{s}(\theta)=\left[\begin{array}[]{c}L_{1}\cos\theta-L_{2}\sin\theta\\ 0\\ L_{1}\sin\theta+L_{2}\cos\theta\end{array}\right],\;\boldsymbol{S}(\theta)=\left[\begin{array}[]{ccc}\cos\theta&0&-\sin\theta\\ 0&1&0\\ \sin\theta&0&\cos\theta\end{array}\right].

As previously discussed, we assume Q0Q_{0} and P2P_{2} is non-deformable whereas P4P_{4} is deformable. This means when the hammer is in contact with string, P4P_{4} moves to P6P_{6}; when contact is absent, the position of P4P_{4} is determined by the shank but not the string. The condition to satisfy that the hammer is in contact with string should be z1(a′′)≤L4z_{1}^{(a^{\prime\prime})}\leq L_{4}, viz. the z′′z^{\prime\prime} direction distance between string point and shank head is less than the static thickness of hammer felt. The hammer felt compression is then

ϑ⁡(θ)={𝒙1(a′′)−𝑳4,z1(a′′)≤L4𝟎,z0(a′′)>L4\boldsymbol{\vartheta}(\theta)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(a^{\prime\prime})}-\boldsymbol{L}_{4},\;z_{1}^{(a^{\prime\prime})}\leq L_{4}\\ \boldsymbol{0},\;z_{0}^{(a^{\prime\prime})}>L_{4}\end{array}\right. (6.19)

where 𝑳4=[0,0,L4]⊤\boldsymbol{L}_{4}=[0,0,L_{4}]^{\top}; negative value of ϑi\vartheta_{i} means the hammer felt is compressed towards the negative direction of xi′′x_{i}^{\prime\prime} axis, and vice versa. Due to compression, the hammer felt exerts an interaction force 𝑭(a′′)​(θ)=[F1(a′′),F2(a′′),F3(a′′)]⊤\boldsymbol{F}^{(a^{\prime\prime})}(\theta)=[F_{1}^{(a^{\prime\prime})},F_{2}^{(a^{\prime\prime})},F_{3}^{(a^{\prime\prime})}]^{\top} (in x′′​y′′​z′′x^{\prime\prime}y^{\prime\prime}z^{\prime\prime} system) on the string. Reciprocally, the hammer felt suffers −𝑭(a′′)-\boldsymbol{F}^{(a^{\prime\prime})} from the string according to Newton’s third law55 5 Note that we ignore here the string’s normal and tangent stress and prestress on the interaction surface exerting on the hammer felt (as well as the relevant strain on the string side), which should already be zero per the Neumann boundary condition specified in (2.14) if DOFs are given to string displacements on this surface. Even if they should not be zero, it is relatively acceptable to ignore them as they are probably less contributive than the hammer’s compression force. Treating them as non-zero would require imposing Dirichlet boundary conditions on some relevant DOFs of the string’s side, which is a computational challenge.. Based on [11], the hammer-string interaction force in the xi′′x^{\prime\prime}_{i} axis is modeled as a nonlinear function of compression as

Fi(a′′)=−sgn(ϑi)[ki|ϑi|pi+riki∂t(|ϑi|pi)],i=1,2,3,F_{i}^{(a^{\prime\prime})}=-\mathrm{sgn}(\vartheta_{i})\left[k_{i}|\vartheta_{i}|^{p_{i}}+r_{i}k_{i}\partial_{t}\left(|\vartheta_{i}|^{p_{i}}\right)\right],\;i=1,2,3, (6.20)

where kik_{i} is the stiffness of hammer felt; pip_{i} is a positive exponent accounting for nonlinearity; rir_{i} is the relaxation coefficient accounting for the hammer’s hysteretic and dissipative behaviour; function sgn⁡(⋅)\mathrm{sgn}(\cdot) returns the sign of a real number. Converting the interaction force to x′​y′​z′x^{\prime}y^{\prime}z^{\prime} and x′​y′​z′x^{\prime}y^{\prime}z^{\prime} coordinates yields 𝑭(a′)=𝑺⁡(θ)​𝑭(a′′)\boldsymbol{F}^{(a^{\prime})}=\boldsymbol{S}(\theta)\boldsymbol{F}^{(a^{\prime\prime})} and 𝑭(a)=𝑹0⊤​𝑭(a′)\boldsymbol{F}^{(a)}=\boldsymbol{R}_{0}^{\top}\boldsymbol{F}^{(a^{\prime})}.

To couple the hammer force with string motion, we need equations in the x′​y′​z′x^{\prime}y^{\prime}z^{\prime} system governing the motion of hammer shank, a rigid body. Denote the coordinates of shank mass centre P0P_{0}, shank rotation centre P1P_{1}, shank head P2P_{2} in the x′​y′​z′x^{\prime}y^{\prime}z^{\prime} system as 𝒙0(d′)\boldsymbol{x}_{0}^{(d^{\prime})}, 𝒙1(d′)\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(d^{\prime})}, 𝒙2(d′)\boldsymbol{x}_{2}^{(d^{\prime})} respectively. It can be found that 𝒙0(d′)=[L0​cos⁡(β0+θ),0,L0​sin⁡(β0+θ)]⊤\boldsymbol{x}_{0}^{(d^{\prime})}=[L_{0}\cos(\beta_{0}+\theta),0,L_{0}\sin(\beta_{0}+\theta)]^{\top} and 𝒙2(d′)=𝒔⁡(θ)\boldsymbol{x}_{2}^{(d^{\prime})}=\boldsymbol{s}(\theta), where β0\beta_{0} is the angle of P1​P0→\overrightarrow{P_{1}P_{0}} to the P1​P3→\overrightarrow{P_{1}P_{3}}. Define the total mass and homogenous line density of the hammer shank as mm, ρ\rho. It can be found that m=ρ⁡(L1+L2)m=\rho(L_{1}+L_{2}), and the axis-free position of center of mass P0P_{0} projected on P1​P3P_{1}P_{3} and P2​P3P_{2}P_{3} are (12​L12+L1​L2)/(L1+L2)(\frac{1}{2}L_{1}^{2}+L_{1}L_{2})/(L_{1}+L_{2}) and 12​L22/(L1+L2)\frac{1}{2}L_{2}^{2}/(L_{1}+L_{2}) respectively. It is obvious that the shank as a rigid body suffers these forces: string reaction force 𝑭(d′′)=−𝑭(a′′)\boldsymbol{F}^{(d^{\prime\prime})}=-\boldsymbol{F}^{(a^{\prime\prime})} at P2P_{2}; a rotation constraint force at P1P_{1}, which has zero torque with respect to the y′y^{\prime} axis; gravity [0,0,−m​g]⊤[0,0,-mg]^{\top} at P0P_{0}, where gg is the scalar gravitational acceleration. It follows that the total torque with respect to the y′y^{\prime} axis is m​g​L0​cos⁡(β0+θ)+𝒍⋅𝑭(d′′)​(θ)mgL_{0}\cos(\beta_{0}+\theta)+\boldsymbol{l}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{(d^{\prime\prime})}(\theta) (only 1 dimension of torque is needed here), where 𝒍=[L2,0,−L1]⊤\boldsymbol{l}=[L_{2},0,-L_{1}]^{\top}; the moment of inertia with respect to the y′′y^{\prime\prime} axis, denoted II, is

I=∫0L1ρ​l2​𝑑l+∫0L2ρ⁡(l2+L12)​𝑑l=ρ⁡(13​L13+13​L23+L12​L2)I=\int_{0}^{L_{1}}\rho l^{2}\mathrm{d}l+\int_{0}^{L_{2}}\rho\left(l^{2}+L_{1}^{2}\right)\mathrm{d}l=\rho\left(\frac{1}{3}L_{1}^{3}+\frac{1}{3}L_{2}^{3}+L_{1}^{2}L_{2}\right) (6.21)

which does not depend on θ\theta. Applying Newton’s second law for rotation, the differential equation of hammer shank motion is

I​θ¨=−μ​θ˙+m​g​L0​cos⁡(β0+θ)+𝒍⋅𝑭(d′′)​(θ),I\ddot{\theta}=-\mu\dot{\theta}+mgL_{0}\cos(\beta_{0}+\theta)+\boldsymbol{l}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{(d^{\prime\prime})}(\theta), (6.22)

where −μ​θ˙-\mu\dot{\theta} is the simplified damping force. Here t=0t=0 is the moment when the felt head first contacts the string and compression is still zero, and initial angle and angular velocity at this time should be known.

From the aforementioned deductions, we can abstract the hammer-string interaction force 𝑭(e)\boldsymbol{F}^{(e)} as a nonlinear operator ℱ⁡(𝒖0(a),θ):(ℝ3,ℝ)→ℝ3\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{u}_{0}^{(a)},\theta):(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{R})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3}. This force should be added to the rhs of (2.11) as a non-conservative force. Then, (2.11) and (6.22) forms 2 sets of coupled equations for 2 sets of variables (𝒖(a),θ)(\boldsymbol{u}^{(a)},\theta), which provides a foundation for obtaining a solution theoretically. Due to the highly nonlinear nature of hammer-string coupling, particularly in that Taylor series approximation may not work well for potentially non-smooth functions in (6.20), it would be inappropriate to use the common perturbation method. In section 7.2 we shall introduce an explicit time discretization method to efficiently solve the hammer-string coupling.

6.1.2 One hammer striking two or three strings

The case of one hammer striking multiple, say three strings can simply be treated it as if three independent felt heads were striking their corresponding strings. Three independent interaction forces 𝑭i=1,2,3(e′)\boldsymbol{F}_{i=1,2,3}^{(e^{\prime})} are computed from three independent compressions. The string force exerted on the shank is the sum 𝑭(d′)=−∑i=13𝑭i(e′)\boldsymbol{F}^{(d^{\prime})}=-\sum_{i=1}^{3}\boldsymbol{F}_{i}^{(e^{\prime})}, assuming the 3 compression forces apply to the same point of shank head. However, this approach may lose the dynamic interaction between different striking points of the hammer felt.

A 3D hammer model may be more accurate in capturing the interplay of different hammer striking points and the different positions of compression forces. The hammer felt is now modeled as a 3D elastic material with space discretization. Two kinds of spacial boundaries consist in the hammer felt: one contains the felt’s 3 potential contact points with the 3 strings, represented as P4,iP_{4,i} with coordinates 𝒙4,i=1,2,3(e′′)\boldsymbol{x}_{4,i=1,2,3}^{(e^{\prime\prime})}; another is the contact surface Γ1(e′′)∈ℝ2\Gamma_{1}^{(e^{\prime\prime})}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} with the hammer shank. The hammer shank is considered as a rigid 3D object, which means no inner space discretization is needed for it. Above all, one needs to pay attention to the choice of coordinate system for the 3D geometry of felt. A recommended choice here is the dynamic x′′​y′′​z′′x^{\prime\prime}y^{\prime\prime}z^{\prime\prime} system, which eliminates the felt’s rigid body movement component and is thus suitable for FEM computation. Also, displacement fields 𝒖(e′′)​(𝒙(e′′),t)\boldsymbol{u}^{(e^{\prime\prime})}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(e^{\prime\prime})},t) for hammer felt and 𝒖(d′′)​(𝒙(d′′),t)\boldsymbol{u}^{(d^{\prime\prime})}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(d^{\prime\prime})},t) for hammer shank need to be defined.

For more realistic modeling that the contact is dynamically distributed over a region rather than occurring at only some dimensionless points, readers can refer to appendix C which describes an iterative algorithm for contact problems directly integrated into FEM, supporting time-varying contact boundary and boundary coupling. Another more analytical (but also seems more simplified) approach for contact problems was introduced in [35], where additional dynamic variables including pressure, density, stiffness and damping of the contact surface along with their governing equations are formulated.

Derivation of the felt compression dynamics is now based on the 3D elastic material model and soundboard model previously introduced, without the need for modeling prestress. We first consider the boundary conditions needed for the felt model. Denote the coordinate of Q1,iQ_{1,i} in the x′′​y′′​z′′x^{\prime\prime}y^{\prime\prime}z^{\prime\prime} system as 𝒙1,i(a′′)\boldsymbol{x}_{1,i}^{(a^{\prime\prime})}, which can be computed similar to (6.1.1). To represent hammer felt compression, Dirichlet boundary condition should be imposed on these 3 contact points as

𝒖(e′′)​(𝒙4,i(e′′),t)={𝒙1,i(a′′)−𝒙4,i(e′′),z1,i(a′′)≤L4𝟎,z1,i(a′′)>L4,\boldsymbol{u}^{(e^{\prime\prime})}(\boldsymbol{x}_{4,i}^{(e^{\prime\prime})},t)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\boldsymbol{x}_{1,i}^{(a^{\prime\prime})}-\boldsymbol{x}_{4,i}^{(e^{\prime\prime})},\;z_{1,i}^{(a^{\prime\prime})}\leq L_{4}\\ \boldsymbol{0},\;z_{1,i}^{(a^{\prime\prime})}>L_{4}\end{array}\right., (6.23)

where z1,i(a′′)≤L4z_{1,i}^{(a^{\prime\prime})}\leq L_{4} means contact is present and otherwise not. This determined displacement would occur on the rhs of system ODEs like (2.42) as a source term. It is assumed without contact, not only P4,iP_{4,i} but also the entire felt will not experience deformation; with contact, the position of P4,iP_{4,i}, i.e. P6,iP_{6,i}, is the same as Q1,iQ_{1,i}, triggering motion and compression of the hammer felt. However, this assumption is a simplification that when the hammer felt leaves the string, its compression immediately recovers, and may result in a problem that Neumann boundary condition is not satisfied at P4,iP_{4,i} when there is no contact. For a more accurate treatment of the contact boundary problem, readers can go to appendix C. There we describe an elastic-rigid 3D contact algorithm able to account for the time-varying contact surface and the time-varying switch between Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions, but with increased algorithmic complexity and numeric convergence uncertainty. As for another boundary Γ1(e′′)\Gamma_{1}^{(e^{\prime\prime})} which interfaces the shank, Dirichlet boundary condition should be imposed on as

𝒖(e′′)​(𝒙(e′′),t)=𝟎,𝒙(e′′)∈Γ1(e′′),\boldsymbol{u}^{(e^{\prime\prime})}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(e^{\prime\prime})},t)=\boldsymbol{0},\;\boldsymbol{x}^{(e^{\prime\prime})}\in\Gamma_{1}^{(e^{\prime\prime})}, (6.24)

because the rigid shank should have no deformation.

We then consider the dynamics of string and shank impacted by the felt. At the contact point with string, the felt’s nonzero surface forces 𝑮(e′′)​(𝒙4,i(e′′),t)\boldsymbol{G}^{(e^{\prime\prime})}(\boldsymbol{x}_{4,i}^{(e^{\prime\prime})},t) should be transmitted to the string as

𝑭i(a)=−[0Z12Z13Z12Z22Z23Z13Z23Z33]​[111],\displaystyle\boldsymbol{F}_{i}^{(a)}=-\left[\begin{array}[]{ccc}0&Z_{12}&Z_{13}\\ Z_{12}&Z_{22}&Z_{23}\\ Z_{13}&Z_{23}&Z_{33}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}1\\ 1\\ 1\end{array}\right],
{Zi​j}=𝑹0⊤​𝑹​(θ)⊤​𝑮(e′′)​(𝒙4,i(e′′),t)​𝑹​(θ)​𝑹0,\displaystyle\left\{Z_{ij}\right\}=\boldsymbol{R}_{0}^{\top}\boldsymbol{R}(\theta)^{\top}\boldsymbol{G}^{(e^{\prime\prime})}(\boldsymbol{x}_{4,i}^{(e^{\prime\prime})},t)\boldsymbol{R}(\theta)\boldsymbol{R}_{0}, (6.31)

where Z11Z_{11} is not transmitted considering that the hammer felt seems to have no direct contact with the string’s surface whose normal is in the xx axis (longitudinal direction). As for the felt’s surface force exerting on the shank along the boundary Γ1(e′′)=Γ1(d′′)\Gamma_{1}^{(e^{\prime\prime})}=\Gamma_{1}^{(d^{\prime\prime})}, previous practice of directly transmitting the felt-string interaction force to the shank is not applicable here due to the 3D nature of felt and shank. For a point 𝒙(e′′)=𝒙(d′′)\boldsymbol{x}^{(e^{\prime\prime})}=\boldsymbol{x}^{(d^{\prime\prime})} in Γ1(e′′)\Gamma_{1}^{(e^{\prime\prime})}, with 𝒏(e′′)​(𝒙(e′′))\boldsymbol{n}^{(e^{\prime\prime})}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(e^{\prime\prime})}) as the outward normal of its tangent plane, the felt would exert a surface force

𝑭(d′′)​(𝒙(d′′),t)=−𝑮(e′′)​(𝒙(e′′),t)​𝒏(e′′)​(𝒙(e′′))\boldsymbol{F}^{(d^{\prime\prime})}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(d^{\prime\prime})},t)=-\boldsymbol{G}^{(e^{\prime\prime})}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(e^{\prime\prime})},t)\boldsymbol{n}^{(e^{\prime\prime})}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(e^{\prime\prime})}) (6.32)

on the shank. Then the total contribution of felt force to the torque of shank with respect to the y′′y^{\prime\prime} axis is

T1​(θ)\displaystyle T_{1}(\theta) =∫Γ1(d′)(𝑬0​𝑭(d′)​(𝒙(d′),t)⋅𝒙(d′))​𝑑V\displaystyle=\int_{\Gamma_{1}^{(d^{\prime})}}\left(\boldsymbol{E}_{0}\boldsymbol{F}^{(d^{\prime})}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(d^{\prime})},t)\cdot\boldsymbol{x}^{(d^{\prime})}\right)\mathrm{d}V
=∫Γ1(d′′)[𝑬0​𝑺​(θ)​𝑭(d′′)​(𝒙(d′′),t)⋅(𝒔⁡(θ)+𝑺⁡(θ)​𝒙(d′′))]​𝑑V\displaystyle=\int_{\Gamma_{1}^{(d^{\prime\prime})}}\left[\boldsymbol{E}_{0}\boldsymbol{S}(\theta)\boldsymbol{F}^{(d^{\prime\prime})}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(d^{\prime\prime})},t)\cdot\left(\boldsymbol{s}(\theta)+\boldsymbol{S}(\theta)\boldsymbol{x}^{(d^{\prime\prime})}\right)\right]\mathrm{d}V
=∫Γ1(d′′)[𝑭(d′′)​(𝒙(d′′),t)⋅(𝒍+𝑬​𝒙(d′′))]​𝑑V,\displaystyle=\int_{\Gamma_{1}^{(d^{\prime\prime})}}\left[\boldsymbol{F}^{(d^{\prime\prime})}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(d^{\prime\prime})},t)\cdot\left(\boldsymbol{l}+\boldsymbol{E}\boldsymbol{x}^{(d^{\prime\prime})}\right)\right]\mathrm{d}V, (6.33)

where

𝒍=[L20−L1],𝑬0=[00−1000100],𝑬=[001000−100]\boldsymbol{l}=\left[\begin{array}[]{c}L_{2}\\ 0\\ -L_{1}\end{array}\right],\boldsymbol{E}_{0}=\left[\begin{array}[]{ccc}0&0&-1\\ 0&0&0\\ 1&0&0\end{array}\right],\boldsymbol{E}=\left[\begin{array}[]{ccc}0&0&1\\ 0&0&0\\ -1&0&0\end{array}\right] (6.34)

are constant quantities. Note that the only dependence of T1T_{1} on θ\theta, though not explicitly written, consists in 𝑭(d′′)​(𝒙(d′′),t)\boldsymbol{F}^{(d^{\prime\prime})}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(d^{\prime\prime})},t), tracing back to the conversion from x​y​zxyz to x′′​y′′​z′′x^{\prime\prime}y^{\prime\prime}z^{\prime\prime} for string displacements. The total contribution of gravity to the torque of shank with respect to the y′′y^{\prime\prime} axis is still m​g​L0​cos⁡(β0+θ)mgL_{0}\cos(\beta_{0}+\theta) if no relevant modifications are made when switching to the 3D hammer model. The moment of inertia with respect to the y′′y^{\prime\prime} axis, constant through time, is

I=∫Ω(d′)ρ⁡(x2+z2)​𝑑V,I=\int_{\Omega^{(d^{\prime})}}\rho\left(x^{2}+z^{2}\right)\mathrm{d}V, (6.35)

where Ω(d′)∈ℝ3\Omega^{(d^{\prime})}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} is the shank’s volume domain. Applying Newton’s second law for rotation, the differential equation of hammer shank motion is

I​θ¨=−μ​θ˙+m​g​L0​cos⁡(β0+θ)+T1​(θ).I\ddot{\theta}=-\mu\dot{\theta}+mgL_{0}\cos(\beta_{0}+\theta)+T_{1}(\theta). (6.36)

Now the whole model of 3D hammer-string coupling has been established. The felt-string interaction force 𝑭i(e)\boldsymbol{F}_{i}^{(e)} in (6.31) is computed from the 3D hammer felt model with Dirichlet boundary conditions (6.23) (6.24), and added to the rhs of (2.11) as a non-conservative force. Then, (2.11) and (6.36) forms 2 sets of coupled equations for 2 sets of variables (𝒖(a),θ)(\boldsymbol{u}^{(a)},\theta), which provides a foundation for obtaining a solution theoretically. Despite the linearity of 3D elasticity model, the felt’s force on the string is still nonlinear because of the interaction judging condition.

6.2 Model for string-soundboard coupling

Piano strings are coupled to the soundboard’s bridge part, which terminates and transmits string vibration to the soundboard. Figure 6 visualizes this coupling at the bridge from 3 perspectives, where x​y​zxyz and x′​y′​z′x^{\prime}y^{\prime}z^{\prime} are the coordinate systems for soundboard and string respectively. Converting a vector (not a point) 𝒗\boldsymbol{v} in the x​y​zxyz system into 𝒗′\boldsymbol{v}^{\prime} in the x′​y′​z′x^{\prime}y^{\prime}z^{\prime} system, according to the angles α\alpha and β\beta marked in figure 6, yields 𝒗′=𝑹​𝒗\boldsymbol{v}^{\prime}=\boldsymbol{R}\boldsymbol{v} where 𝑹=𝑹1​𝑹2\boldsymbol{R}=\boldsymbol{R}_{1}\boldsymbol{R}_{2} and

𝑹1=[cos⁡α0sin⁡α010−sin⁡α0cos⁡α],𝑹2=[cos⁡βsin⁡β0−sin⁡βcos⁡β0001]\boldsymbol{R}_{1}=\left[\begin{array}[]{ccc}\cos\alpha&0&\sin\alpha\\ 0&1&0\\ -\sin\alpha&0&\cos\alpha\end{array}\right],\;\boldsymbol{R}_{2}=\left[\begin{array}[]{ccc}\cos\beta&\sin\beta&0\\ -\sin\beta&\cos\beta&0\\ 0&0&1\end{array}\right] (6.37)

are the rotation matrices. The orthogonal property of rotation matrix yields 𝒗=𝑹⊤​𝒗′\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{R}^{\top}\boldsymbol{v}^{\prime}.

We conjecture from observations that the string-soundboard coupling is achieved via several mechanisms. The first mechanism is “bridge hump coupling”, as illustrated in the side perspective of figure 6. The middle part of bridge is constructed a bit higher than the agraffe, the starting point of the speaking string. As a result, the string experiences some upward pressure from the bridge and the bridge experiences some downward pressure from the string, both statically and dynamically. The second mechanism is “bridge pin horizontal coupling”, as illustrated in the top perspective of figure 6. Two bridge pins for one string are drilled into the bridge at positions that would bend the string a bit horizontally, bringing mutual horizontal tension between the string and bridge, and restricting the string’s horizontal movement. Made of hard metal like steel, brass or even titanium, the bridge pins can be treated as rigid bodies with zero strain and stress. The third mechanism is “bridge pin vertical coupling”, as illustrated in the front perspective of figure 6. The two bridge pins lean towards their respective string sides, blocking the string from moving upwards beyond the pins. Also, the notches of bridge ensure that bridge hump coupling and bridge pin coupling occur at almost the same position, viz. the front bridge pin (the one closer to the agraffe).

On the string’s side, the coupling point is defined as 𝒙1(a)=[L1(a),0,−r(a)]⊤\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(a)}=[L_{1}^{(a)},0,-r^{(a)}]^{\top}, the lowest point of string at the front pin. While other relevant points for coupling may be [L1(a),−r(a),0]⊤[L_{1}^{(a)},-r^{(a)},0]^{\top}, the closest point of string to the bridge pin, the string’s displacements and surface forces at these points are identical, assuming u(a)u^{(a)} does not vary with y(a)y^{(a)} or z(a)z^{(a)} at x(a)=L1(a)x^{(a)}=L_{1}^{(a)} (no rotation) for simplicity66 6 This is also true for the string’s central point 𝒙1(a)=[L1(a),0,0]⊤\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(a)}=[L_{1}^{(a)},0,0]^{\top} previously defined.. The coordinate of this coupling point on the soundboard’s side is denoted 𝒙1(b)\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(b)}.

6.2.1 Static coupling

For coupling before motion is initiated, the string and soundboard should have non-zero prestress fields that attain static balance. It is sufficient to specify that the string prestress only acts perpendicular to its cross-sections and is constant through its speaking length. This means in the string’s tension matrix 𝑻(a)\boldsymbol{T}^{(a)}, T11T_{11} is a constant and other entries are zero, immediately satisfying the static balance. For the soundboard, a full space dependent tension matrix 𝑻(b)\boldsymbol{T}^{(b)} with 6 unique elements is necessary. The static balance condition can then be expressed as 3 partial differential equations

∇⋅𝑻(b)=𝟎,\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{T}^{(b)}=\boldsymbol{0}, (6.38)

which can be solved numerically by FEM using nodal surface forces as time-independent DOFs. Nonetheless, continuity between string and soundboard tension fields is required. To write the continuity equations, we define an intermediate coordinate system x′′​y′′​z′′x^{\prime\prime}y^{\prime\prime}z^{\prime\prime} resulting from rotating the x′​y′​z′x^{\prime}y^{\prime}z^{\prime} system by 𝑹1⊤\boldsymbol{R}_{1}^{\top} or rotating the x​y​zxyz system by 𝑹2\boldsymbol{R}_{2}, as marked blue in figure 6. At the coupling point, the string’s tension on surfaces with outward normals in the y′′y^{\prime\prime} and z′′z^{\prime\prime} axes exert on the bridge, whereas that in the x′′x^{\prime\prime} axis exerts on the farther hitch pins that seem to not connect the soundboard. This leads to one Dirichlet boundary condition for each string coupled to the soundboard as

(𝑹2​𝑻(b)​(𝒙1(b))​𝑹2⊤)[22,33,12,13,23]=(𝑹1⊤​𝑻(a)​(𝒙1(a))​𝑹1)[22,33,12,13,23],\left(\boldsymbol{R}_{2}\boldsymbol{T}^{(b)}(\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(b)})\boldsymbol{R}_{2}^{\top}\right)_{[22,33,12,13,23]}=\left(\boldsymbol{R}_{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{T}^{(a)}(\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(a)})\boldsymbol{R}_{1}\right)_{[22,33,12,13,23]}, (6.39)

where subscript [i1,i2,…]{}_{[i_{1},i_{2},...]} means taking vector or matrix elements at indices i1,i2,…i_{1},i_{2},... to form a vector. This condition can be deduced into 5 equations, leaving 1 DOF for the coupling point.

6.2.2 Dynamic coupling

For coupling in motion, the string transmits its surface forces (dynamic prestress, stress and damping force) to the soundboard. At coupling point, the string’s total surface force, excluding the static prestress which is already accounted for on the soundboard’s side, is 𝑮(a)​(𝒙1,t)\boldsymbol{G}^{(a)}(\boldsymbol{x}_{1},t). Similar to static coupling, only forces on surfaces with outward normals in the y′′y^{\prime\prime} and z′′z^{\prime\prime} axes are transmitted to the soundboard at the coupling point. This leads to

𝑭(b)​(𝒙(b),t)=δ⁡(𝒙(b)−𝒙1(b))​(𝑹2⊤​[0Z12Z13Z12Z22Z23Z13Z23Z33]​𝑹2)​[111],\displaystyle\boldsymbol{F}^{(b)}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(b)},t)=\delta\left(\boldsymbol{x}^{(b)}-\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(b)}\right)\left(\boldsymbol{R}_{2}^{\top}\left[\begin{array}[]{ccc}0&Z_{12}&Z_{13}\\ Z_{12}&Z_{22}&Z_{23}\\ Z_{13}&Z_{23}&Z_{33}\end{array}\right]\boldsymbol{R}_{2}\right)\left[\begin{array}[]{c}1\\ 1\\ 1\end{array}\right],
{Zi​j}=𝑹1⊤​𝑮(a)​(𝒙1(a),t)​𝑹1,\displaystyle\left\{Z_{ij}\right\}=\boldsymbol{R}_{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{G}^{(a)}(\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(a)},t)\boldsymbol{R}_{1}, (6.46)

where δ⁡(𝒙)\delta(\boldsymbol{x}) is a 3D Dirac delta function indicating a point load. The above equations treats the string’s surface force as a non-conservative force input to the soundboard system.

Another coupling condition arising from observation is that the string and soundboard should have the same y′′y^{\prime\prime} and z′′z^{\prime\prime} direction displacements77 7 Here displacement continuity should be equivalent to velocity continuity, since both the string’s and soundboard’s displacements are based on a [0,0,0]⊤[0,0,0]^{\top} point. at the coupling point, written as

(𝑹1⊤​∂t𝒖(a)​(𝒙1(a),t))[2,3]=(𝑹2​∂t𝒖(b)​(𝒙1(b),t))[2,3].\left(\boldsymbol{R}_{1}^{\top}\partial_{t}\boldsymbol{u}^{(a)}(\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(a)},t)\right)_{[2,3]}=\left(\boldsymbol{R}_{2}\partial_{t}\boldsymbol{u}^{(b)}(\boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{(b)},t)\right)_{[2,3]}. (6.47)

The reason for this is that the the aforementioned three coupling mechanisms constitute support for the string’s surfaces with outward normals in the y′′y^{\prime\prime} and z′′z^{\prime\prime} axes at the coupling point. This may not hold for the x′′x^{\prime\prime} axis, but if it is needed88 8 Maybe in case of high enough viscosity or friction, the string can not slip more than the soundboard in the x′′x^{\prime\prime} direction. Restricting this movement may also make the solution of string’s PDE more stable. This needs to be tested., the subscript [2,3] in above equations can be removed to impose a stronger displacement continuity condition. Anyway, restriction of the string’s x′′x^{\prime\prime} axis (longitudinal) motion is always present at the farther hitch point which may not connect the soundboard, see (4.9). The same-displacement condition also provides a basis for establishing the string’s displacement at the coupling point (Dirichlet boundary condition), so that the string’s PDE (2.11) has an appropriate solution.

6.2.3 More discussions on coupling

String-soundboard coupling exhibits complex mechanisms that we find challenging to discover and describe. Some of these mechanisms that we observe but not covered in the aforementioned coupling model are discussed in this subsection. These discussions may not cover much details of computation due to their complexities.

Firstly, we only specified the coupling point at the bridge’s front pin but ignored the rear pin. As coupling at the rear pin position potentially exists, the string in our model may need to be extented in length to cover the segment between the front pin position 𝒙1=[L1(a),0,−r(a)]⊤\boldsymbol{x}_{1}=[L_{1}^{(a)},0,-r^{(a)}]^{\top} and the rear pin position 𝒙2=[L2(a),0,−r(a)]⊤\boldsymbol{x}_{2}=[L_{2}^{(a)},0,-r^{(a)}]^{\top} (we call it “this segment” is this paragraph). At this segment, the horizontal bending of string may be accouted for in the prestress, but not necessarily represented in the geometrical volume for simplicity. In static state, the prestress field coupling should be computed for this segment paying attention that only at the two pin points are y′′y^{\prime\prime} axis surface forces coupled. In dynamic state, transmission of the string’s surface forces should be computed for this segment, paying attention that only at the two pin points are y′′y^{\prime\prime} axis surface forces transmitted. A maybe more accurate computation of surface force transmission is, that at the two pins only when the string’s y′′y^{\prime\prime} axis surface forces are towards the front or rear pins should they be transmitted, and that at between (excluding) the two pins only when the string’s z′′z^{\prime\prime} axis surface forces are upwards should they be transmitted. This may lead to a highly nonlinear function akin to the case of hammer-string interaction (6.19), and may make imposing boundary conditions tougher due to the inequality rather than equality nature. For displacement coupling at this segment, at the two pins when the string’s y′′y^{\prime\prime} direction displacements should not exceed the pins, whereas the z′′z^{\prime\prime} direction displacements are fully coupled to the pins; at between (excluding) the string’s z′′z^{\prime\prime} direction displacements should not be under the soundboard plane, whereas the y′′y^{\prime\prime} direction displacements are unrestricted.

Secondly, we considered coupling as occurring at a point, but it may actually occur in a small contact surface (we call it “this surface” is this paragraph). In such a case, the Dirichlet boundary condition of prestress field coupling should be specified over this surface; the dynamic surface force transmission should be treated as surface load rather than point load; the Dirichlet boundary condition of displacement coupling should also be specified over this surface.

Thirdly, we still lack geometric details regarding the string’s notable vertical and horizontal bending at the bridge. This bending changes the string’s longitudinal direction, and thereby the 3 directions of vibration. Though string vibration should be terminated at the bridge pin, it seems only at the hitch pin that longitudinal vibration is fully restricted. Therefore, the string’s segment from front bridge pin to hitch pin may require investigation, which may concern the duplex scale phenomena [25]. We can design a multi-segment geometric model for the string, each segment having differently rotated constitutive matrices. Also, the position-dependent static tension can be specified parallel to the central line of each string segment.

Finally, we ignored the soundboard’s normal and tangent surface forces exerting on the string at coupling point. This is similar to the case of hammer-string coupling where the string’s surface forces exerting on the hammer are ignored. This is mainly for practical considerations, as we would want to solve the soundboard’s equations for only once. Since we did not impose Dirichlet boundary condition for the soundboard at each coupling point with the around 200 strings, Neumann boundary conditions apply here restricting the soundboard’s conservative surface forces to be zero at coupling points. It may be acceptable given the intuitive feeling that “string → soundboard” transmission should dominate “soundboard → string” transmission. If the latter is essential, some DOFs may be need to be removed from the coupling point on the soundboard’s side, which is a challenge for imposing Dirichlet boundary condition reasonably for both the string and the soundboard.

6.3 Model for soundboard-air and room-air coupling

Modeling soundboard-air and room-air coupling is crucial for arriving at the final digital audio sound to the listeners. Generally in the context of solid-fluid coupling dynamics, the interaction surface should have continuous normal and tangential velocities, as well as continuous normal and tangential surface forces on both sides [19].

As per section 5, room-air coupling occurs on surface Γ1(f)\Gamma_{1}^{(f)} (room side) and Γ1(c)\Gamma_{1}^{(c)} (air side). Define coordinate transformation 𝒙(f)=𝒓1+𝑹1​𝒙(c)\boldsymbol{x}^{(f)}=\boldsymbol{r}_{1}+\boldsymbol{R}_{1}\boldsymbol{x}^{(c)} from air coordinates to soundboard coordinates, where 𝒓1\boldsymbol{r}_{1} and 𝑹1\boldsymbol{R}_{1} are the shift vector and rotation matrix. We impose Dirichlet boundary condition of velocity continuity that

𝒖(c)​(𝒙(c),t)=𝑹1⊤​𝒖˙(f)​(𝒙(f),t),𝒙(c)∈Γ1(c),𝒙(f)=𝒓1+𝑹1​𝒙(c).\boldsymbol{u}^{(c)}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(c)},t)=\boldsymbol{R}_{1}^{\top}\dot{\boldsymbol{u}}^{(f)}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(f)},t),\;\boldsymbol{x}^{(c)}\in\Gamma_{1}^{(c)},\;\boldsymbol{x}^{(f)}=\boldsymbol{r}_{1}+\boldsymbol{R}_{1}\boldsymbol{x}^{(c)}. (6.48)

We also specify the contribution of air surface force to the room equation’s source term on the rhs of (2.11) as

𝑭1(f)​(𝒙(f),t)=−𝑮(c)​(𝒙(c),t)​𝒏(c)​(𝒙(c)),𝒙(f)∈Γ1(f),𝒙(c)=−𝑹1⊤​𝒓1+𝑹1⊤​𝒙(f),\displaystyle\boldsymbol{F}_{1}^{(f)}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(f)},t)=-\boldsymbol{G}^{(c)}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(c)},t)\boldsymbol{n}^{(c)}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(c)}),\;\boldsymbol{x}^{(f)}\in\Gamma_{1}^{(f)},\;\boldsymbol{x}^{(c)}=-\boldsymbol{R}_{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{r}_{1}+\boldsymbol{R}_{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}^{(f)}, (6.49)

where 𝒏(c)​(𝒙(c))\boldsymbol{n}^{(c)}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(c)}) is the outward normal of the tangent plane of 𝒙(c)\boldsymbol{x}^{(c)}.

As per sections 3 and 5, soundboard-air coupling occurs on surface Γ2(b)\Gamma_{2}^{(b)} (soundboard side) and Γ2(c)\Gamma_{2}^{(c)} (air side). Define coordinate transformation 𝒙(b)=𝒓2+𝑹2​𝒙(c)\boldsymbol{x}^{(b)}=\boldsymbol{r}_{2}+\boldsymbol{R}_{2}\boldsymbol{x}^{(c)} from air coordinates to soundboard coordinates, where 𝒓2\boldsymbol{r}_{2} and 𝑹2\boldsymbol{R}_{2} are the shift vector and rotation matrix. We impose Dirichlet boundary condition of velocity continuity that

𝒖(c)​(𝒙(c),t)=𝑹2⊤​𝒖˙(b)​(𝒙(b),t),𝒙(c)∈Γ2(c),𝒙(b)=𝒓2+𝑹2​𝒙(c).\boldsymbol{u}^{(c)}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(c)},t)=\boldsymbol{R}_{2}^{\top}\dot{\boldsymbol{u}}^{(b)}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(b)},t),\;\boldsymbol{x}^{(c)}\in\Gamma_{2}^{(c)},\;\boldsymbol{x}^{(b)}=\boldsymbol{r}_{2}+\boldsymbol{R}_{2}\boldsymbol{x}^{(c)}. (6.50)

We also specify the contribution of air surface force to the soundboard equation’s source term on the rhs of (2.11) as

𝑭1(b)​(𝒙(b),t)=−𝑮(c)​(𝒙(c),t)​𝒏(c)​(𝒙(c)),𝒙(b)∈Γ2(b),𝒙(c)=−𝑹2⊤​𝒓2+𝑹2⊤​𝒙(b),\displaystyle\boldsymbol{F}_{1}^{(b)}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(b)},t)=-\boldsymbol{G}^{(c)}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(c)},t)\boldsymbol{n}^{(c)}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(c)}),\;\boldsymbol{x}^{(b)}\in\Gamma_{2}^{(b)},\;\boldsymbol{x}^{(c)}=-\boldsymbol{R}_{2}^{\top}\boldsymbol{r}_{2}+\boldsymbol{R}_{2}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}^{(b)}, (6.51)

where 𝒏(c)​(𝒙(c))\boldsymbol{n}^{(c)}(\boldsymbol{x}^{(c)}) is the outward normal of the tangent plane of 𝒙(c)\boldsymbol{x}^{(c)}.

7 Numeric schemes

7.1 Modal superposition method for solving coupled ODEs

7.1.1 Modal transformation of second-order ODEs

For solving coupled second-order ODEs like (2.42), time discretization using finite-difference is a direct approach. However, given that damping matrix is diagonalizable by the mass and stiffness matrices, decoupling and dimension reduction of the system by means of modal superposition is preferred. To do so, we first define the following eigenvalue problem

𝑲​ϕi=λi​𝑴​ϕi⟺𝑴−1​𝑲​ϕi=λi​ϕi​(i=1,…,N),\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i}=\lambda_{i}\boldsymbol{M}\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i}\Longleftrightarrow\boldsymbol{M}^{-1}\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i}=\lambda_{i}\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i}\;(i=1,...,N), (7.1)

and the eigen decomposition

𝑲=𝑴​𝚽​𝚲​𝚽−1⟺𝑴−1​𝑲=𝚽​𝚲​𝚽−1,\boldsymbol{K}=\boldsymbol{M}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-1}\Longleftrightarrow\boldsymbol{M}^{-1}\boldsymbol{K}=\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-1}, (7.2)

where λi\lambda_{i} is a (maybe complex) eigenvalue, ϕi\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i} is a N×1N\times 1 (maybe complex) eigenvector, 𝚲=diag⁡(λ1,…,λN)\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},...,\lambda_{N}) is a diagonal matrix of eigenvalues, 𝚽=[ϕ1,…,ϕN]\boldsymbol{\Phi}=[\boldsymbol{\phi}_{1},...,\boldsymbol{\phi}_{N}] is a N×NN\times N matrix of eigenvectors. Note that since both 𝑴\boldsymbol{M} and 𝑲\boldsymbol{K} are sparse matrices with large dimensions, it is preferrable to solve the generalized eigenvalue problem on the left side of (7.1), avoiding explicit inversion of 𝑴\boldsymbol{M} that would otherwise result in a large dense matrix. We can leverage existing softwares of sparse eigensolvers like Arpack and FEAST to solve the generalized eigenvalue problem. Nevertheless, for solving ODEs of the acoustic system with large DOFs, it may be unwise to store all rows of eigenvectors at the same time which may otherwise lead to memory overload. A re-implementation of existing sparse eigensolver algorithms may be desired so as to store partial rows or columns of eigenvectors in a “rolling” way.

Since eigenvectors are linearly independent, that is to say 𝚽\boldsymbol{\Phi} is invertible, we can write the solution in the form 𝝃⁡(t)=𝚽​𝒒​(t)\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)=\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{q}(t) where 𝒒⁡(t)\boldsymbol{q}(t) is an N×1N\times 1 vector we call as modal DOFs. Note here 𝝃⁡(t)\boldsymbol{\xi}(t) should be real (in the complex domain), but 𝒒⁡(t)\boldsymbol{q}(t) may be complex because 𝚽−1\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-1} may be complex. Then (2.42) can be decoupled as

𝑴​𝚽​𝒒¨​(t)+2​μ​𝑲​𝚽​𝒒˙​(t)+𝑲​𝚽​𝒒​(t)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{M}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\ddot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t)+2\mu\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t)+\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{q}(t) =𝒇⁡(t)\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{f}(t) (7.3a)
𝚽H​𝑴​𝚽​𝒒¨​(t)+2​μ​𝚽H​𝑲​𝚽​𝒒˙​(t)+𝚽H​𝑲​𝚽​𝒒​(t)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\mathrm{H}}\boldsymbol{M}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\ddot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t)+2\mu\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\mathrm{H}}\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t)+\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\mathrm{H}}\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{q}(t) =𝚽H​𝒇​(t)\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\mathrm{H}}\boldsymbol{f}(t) (7.3b)
𝑴¯​𝒒¨​(t)+2​μ​𝑴¯​𝚲​𝒒˙​(t)+𝑴¯​𝚲​𝒒​(t)\displaystyle\bar{\boldsymbol{M}}\ddot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t)+2\mu\bar{\boldsymbol{M}}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t)+\bar{\boldsymbol{M}}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{q}(t) =𝚽H​𝒇​(t)\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\mathrm{H}}\boldsymbol{f}(t) (7.3c)
𝒒¨​(t)+2​μ​𝚲​𝒒˙​(t)+𝚲​𝒒​(t)\displaystyle\ddot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t)+2\mu\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t)+\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{q}(t) =𝒑⁡(t)\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{p}(t) (7.3d)

where

𝑴¯=𝚽H​𝑴​𝚽,𝒑⁡(t)=𝑴¯−1​𝚽H​𝒇​(t);\bar{\boldsymbol{M}}=\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\mathrm{H}}\boldsymbol{M}\boldsymbol{\Phi},\;\boldsymbol{p}(t)=\bar{\boldsymbol{M}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\mathrm{H}}\boldsymbol{f}(t); (7.4)

are called the modal mass matrix and the modal force vector respectively. Through eigen decomposition, the NN coupled ODEs have now been transformed into NN uncoupled ODEs. Note that in case the damping matrix can not be diagonalized by the mass and stiffness matrices, we should rewrite the second-order ODEs as first-order ODEs with doubled number of DOFs, so that it can be decoupled as will be shown in section 7.1.2.

It is well-understood that the analytical solution of the ii th uncoupled second-order ODE without the rhs nonhomogenous term is a sinusoidal signal with a single eigenfrequency positively correlated to the magnitude of ii th eigenvalue. Assuming eigenvalues in 𝚲\boldsymbol{\Lambda} are ascendingly sorted by their real magitudes, we can select only the lowest MM eigenvalues and discard the rest, because most human ears are insensitive to eigenfrequencies above a certain threshold (often 10 kHz). This is also for practical considerations that the number of DOFs is often too large for numeric computation, making dimension reduction desirable. Consequently, we obtain a M×1M\times 1 vector 𝒒′​(t)\boldsymbol{q}^{\prime}(t) with only the first MM entries of 𝒒⁡(t)\boldsymbol{q}(t), and the M+1M+1 to NN entries are all approximated as zeros and discarded. Subsituting 𝒒⁡(t)\boldsymbol{q}(t) by 𝒒′​(t)\boldsymbol{q}^{\prime}(t) (more exactly, 𝒒′​(t)\boldsymbol{q}^{\prime}(t) should be padded N−MN-M zeros at the end) in (7.3c), and omitting the last N−MN-M equations and unknowns, yields

𝑺′​𝒒¨′​(t)+2​μ​𝑺′​𝚲′​𝒒˙′​(t)+𝑺′​𝚲′​𝒒′​(t)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{S}^{\prime}\ddot{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}(t)+2\mu\boldsymbol{S}^{\prime}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{\prime}\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}(t)+\boldsymbol{S}^{\prime}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{\prime}\boldsymbol{q}^{\prime}(t) =𝚽′𝒇⊤(t)\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\prime}{}^{\top}\boldsymbol{f}(t) (7.5a)
𝒒¨′​(t)+2​μ​𝚲′​𝒒˙′​(t)+𝚲′​𝒒′​(t)\displaystyle\ddot{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}(t)+2\mu\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{\prime}\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}^{\prime}(t)+\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{\prime}\boldsymbol{q}^{\prime}(t) =𝒑′​(t)\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{p}^{\prime}(t) (7.5b)

where 𝚲′\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{\prime} has dimension M×MM\times M containing the first MM eigenvalues and 𝚽′\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\prime} has dimension N×MN\times M containing the first MM eigenvectors. The large numbe of DOFs is now approximated as the linear combination of a smaller number of modal DOFs as 𝝃⁡(t)≈𝚽′​𝒒′​(t)\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\approx\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\prime}\boldsymbol{q}^{\prime}(t). The reduced modal mass and modal force are

𝑴¯′=𝚽′​𝑴H​𝚽′,𝒑⁡(t)=𝑴¯′​𝚽′−1​𝒇H​(t).\bar{\boldsymbol{M}}^{\prime}=\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\prime}{}^{\mathrm{H}}\boldsymbol{M}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\prime},\;\boldsymbol{p}(t)=\bar{\boldsymbol{M}}^{\prime}{}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\prime}{}^{\mathrm{H}}\boldsymbol{f}(t). (7.6)

For around 2500 modes of the soundboard system as estimated in [10], the fully dense modal mass matrix (128 bit complex type) would require about 95 MB memory which is normally acceptable in both storage and computation aspects. But this dense matrix can be avoided if the mass and stiffness matrices are both symmetric because in this case the eigenvectors can be normalized so that the modal mass matrix equals to an identity matrix, making its inversion much easier. This benefit is achievable in our 3D elastic solid model because the constitutive matrix is symmetric even in the presence of prestres. A symmetric stiffness matrix often means that energy is conserved within the system if there is no other non-conservative forces like damping force.

Now we consider the analytical solution of the ii th uncoupled nonhomogenous ODE

q¨​(t)+2​μ​λ​q˙​(t)+λ​q​(t)=p⁡(t),\ddot{q}(t)+2\mu\lambda\dot{q}(t)+\lambda q(t)=p(t), (7.7)

where the subscripts i and superscripts ′ are dropped for convenience. Applying Laplace transform to this equation yields

s2​Q​(s)+2​μ​λ​s​Q​(s)+λ​Q​(s)\displaystyle s^{2}Q(s)+2\mu\lambda sQ(s)+\lambda Q(s) =P​(s)+Q0​(s),\displaystyle=P(s)+Q_{0}(s),
s2​G​(s)+2​μ​λ​s​G​(s)+λ​G​(s)−G0​(s)\displaystyle s^{2}G(s)+2\mu\lambda sG(s)+\lambda G(s)-G_{0}(s) =1\displaystyle=1
g¨​(t)+2​μ​λ​g˙​(t)+λ​g​(t)\displaystyle\ddot{g}(t)+2\mu\lambda\dot{g}(t)+\lambda g(t) =δ⁡(t)\displaystyle=\delta(t) (7.8)

where ss is a complex variable, δ⁡(t)\delta(t) is the Dirac delta function; the initial parts of Laplace transforming derivatives are defined as

Q0​(s)\displaystyle Q_{0}(s) =s​q​(0)+q˙​(0)+2​μ​λ​q​(0)\displaystyle=sq(0)+\dot{q}(0)+2\mu\lambda q(0)
G0​(s)\displaystyle G_{0}(s) =s​g​(0)+g˙​(0)+2​μ​λ​g​(0);\displaystyle=sg(0)+\dot{g}(0)+2\mu\lambda g(0); (7.9)

the well-known Green’s function (frequency domain), the response to a unit impulse, is defined as

G⁡(s)=Q⁡(s)​[1+G0​(s)]P​(s)+Q0​(s)⇒Q⁡(s)=G⁡(s)​[P⁡(s)+Q0​(s)]1+G0​(s).G(s)=\frac{Q(s)\left[1+G_{0}(s)\right]}{P(s)+Q_{0}(s)}\Rightarrow Q(s)=\frac{G(s)\left[P(s)+Q_{0}(s)\right]}{1+G_{0}(s)}. (7.10)

To solve g⁡(t)g(t), we first specify that response should not exist during zero and negative time, viz. g​(t)=g˙​(t)=0g(t)=\dot{g}(t)=0 for t≤0t\leq 0; then notice when t>0t>0, (7.8) becomes homogenous with solution

g⁡(t)=C1​exp⁡(z1​t)+C2​exp⁡(z2​t),z1,z2=−μ​λ±(μ2​λ−1)​λ.g(t)=C_{1}\exp(z_{1}t)+C_{2}\exp(z_{2}t),\;z_{1},z_{2}=-\mu\lambda\pm\sqrt{(\mu^{2}\lambda-1)\lambda}.

To determine complex constants C1C_{1}, C2C_{2}, we first notice that g⁡(t)g(t) should be continuous at t=0t=0 in the presence of second derivative in (7.8), thus

g⁡(0+)=g⁡(0)⇒C1+C2=0.g(0^{+})=g(0)\Rightarrow C_{1}+C_{2}=0. (7.11)

Then, integrating (7.8) over (−∞,+∞)(-\infty,+\infty) yields

∫−∞+∞[g¨​(t)+2​μ​λ​g˙​(t)+λ​g​(t)]​𝑑t=∫−∞+∞δ⁡(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\left[\ddot{g}(t)+2\mu\lambda\dot{g}(t)+\lambda g(t)\right]\mathrm{d}t=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\delta(t)\mathrm{d}t
⇒\displaystyle\Rightarrow ∫0−0+g¨​(t)​𝑑t=g˙​(0+)−g˙​(0−)=g˙​(0+)=1\displaystyle\int_{0^{-}}^{0^{+}}\ddot{g}(t)\mathrm{d}t=\dot{g}(0^{+})-\dot{g}(0^{-})=\dot{g}(0^{+})=1

which is the so-called jump discontinuity condition for first derivative; the continuity condition for the zero-order has been applied again here. From (7.11) (7.12) the complex constants are found to be

C1=1z1−z2,C2=1z2−z1.C_{1}=\frac{1}{z_{1}-z_{2}},\;C_{2}=\frac{1}{z_{2}-z_{1}}. (7.13)

Subsituting g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0 and g˙​(0)=0\dot{g}(0)=0 into (7.9) yields G0​(s)=0G_{0}(s)=0. Then from (7.10) we have

Q⁡(s)\displaystyle Q(s) =P⁡(s)​G​(s)+[q˙​(0)+2​μ​λ​q​(0)]​G​(s)+s​q​(0)​G​(s)\displaystyle=P(s)G(s)+\left[\dot{q}(0)+2\mu\lambda q(0)\right]G(s)+sq(0)G(s)
q⁡(t)\displaystyle q(t) =p⁡(t)∗g⁡(t)+[q˙​(0)+2​μ​λ​q​(0)]​g​(t)+q⁡(0)​g˙​(t),\displaystyle=p(t)*g(t)+\left[\dot{q}(0)+2\mu\lambda q(0)\right]g(t)+q(0)\dot{g}(t), (7.14)

where ∗* is the convolution operator over [0,+∞)[0,+\infty). For the general case of initial conditions q​(0)=q˙​(0)=0q(0)=\dot{q}(0)=0, the solution reduces to q⁡(t)=p⁡(t)∗g⁡(t)q(t)=p(t)*g(t). It is now clear that the nonhomogenous ODEs can be solved by convolving the modal force p⁡(t)p(t) (source signal) with the Green’s function g⁡(t)g(t) (response signal), which can be efficiently computed using fast Fourier transform (FFT) convolution in the frequency domain. However, the analytical solution may not be actually useful or efficient in the presence of coupling between systems and the explicit time discretization scheme introduced in section 7.2 will be an alternative. Nevertheless, it provides an understanding of the characteristics of vibration modes.

7.1.2 Modal transformation of first-order ODEs

Solving coupled first-order ODEs like (5.70) by means of modal superposition is similar to the second-order case, and we only discuss some particularities here. Firstly, the eigenvalue problem is defined in the same way for 𝑴\boldsymbol{M} (now for first-order) and 𝑲\boldsymbol{K}. The decoupled ODEs write

𝑴¯​𝒒˙​(t)+𝑴¯​𝚲​𝒒​(t)\displaystyle\bar{\boldsymbol{M}}\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t)+\bar{\boldsymbol{M}}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{q}(t) =𝚽H​𝒇​(t)\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\mathrm{H}}\boldsymbol{f}(t) (7.15a)
𝒒˙​(t)+𝚲​𝒒​(t)\displaystyle\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t)+\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{q}(t) =𝒑⁡(t)\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{p}(t) (7.15b)

where

𝑴¯=𝚽H​𝑴​𝚽,𝒑⁡(t)=𝑴¯−1​𝚽H​𝒇​(t)\bar{\boldsymbol{M}}=\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\mathrm{H}}\boldsymbol{M}\boldsymbol{\Phi},\;\boldsymbol{p}(t)=\bar{\boldsymbol{M}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\mathrm{H}}\boldsymbol{f}(t) (7.16)

are the modal mass and the modal force. Specific attension should be paid to the analytical solution of the ii th uncoupled nonhomogenous ODE

q˙​(t)+λ​q​(t)=p⁡(t).\dot{q}(t)+\lambda q(t)=p(t). (7.17)

Laplace transform yields

s​Q​(s)+λ​Q​(s)\displaystyle sQ(s)+\lambda Q(s) =P⁡(s)+q⁡(0),\displaystyle=P(s)+q(0),
s​G​(s)+λ​G​(s)−g⁡(0)\displaystyle sG(s)+\lambda G(s)-g(0) =1\displaystyle=1
g˙​(t)+λ​g​(t)\displaystyle\dot{g}(t)+\lambda g(t) =δ⁡(t)\displaystyle=\delta(t) (7.18)

where the Green’s function is defined as

G⁡(s)=Q​(s)​[1+g​(0)]P⁡(s)+q⁡(0)⇒Q⁡(s)=G​(s)​[P​(s)+q​(0)]1+g⁡(0).G(s)=\frac{Q(s)\left[1+g(0)\right]}{P(s)+q(0)}\Rightarrow Q(s)=\frac{G(s)\left[P(s)+q(0)\right]}{1+g(0)}. (7.19)

Note that g​(t)=g˙​(t)=0g(t)=\dot{g}(t)=0 for t≤0t\leq 0 is still required, but continuity g⁡(0)=g⁡(0+)g(0)=g(0^{+}) is unnecessary because the highest order of derivative in (7.18) is only one. Nevertheless, continuity of ∫g⁡(t)​𝑑t\int g(t)\mathrm{d}t at t=0t=0 can be easily satisfied because the primitive function can have an arbitrary constant added. Then integrating (7.18), we can find g⁡(0+)=1g(0^{+})=1 and the solution of Green’s function

g⁡(t)=−1λ​exp⁡(−λ​t).g(t)=-\frac{1}{\lambda}\exp(-\lambda t). (7.20)

It follows that

Q⁡(s)\displaystyle Q(s) =P⁡(s)​G​(s)+q⁡(0)​G​(s)\displaystyle=P(s)G(s)+q(0)G(s)
q⁡(t)\displaystyle q(t) =p⁡(t)∗g⁡(t)+q⁡(0)​g​(t),\displaystyle=p(t)*g(t)+q(0)g(t), (7.21)

is the solution of the uncoupled nonhomogenous first-order ODE.

7.2 Explicit time discretization for coupling between systems

Having discussed the weak form ODEs for each subsystem of the physical piano, our question is then how a numerical treatment of coupling between system may be achieved that attains a sensible tradeoff between feasibility and accuracy. For most subsystems presented in the previous sections, there exists an external force term on the rhs of PDEs. This, along with the predetermined displacements on the boundary, form the main contributions to the rhs source term of system ODEs.

Nevertheless, to say “ODEs” here is actually indefensible, because in many coupling cases discussed before the rhs source term 𝒇⁡(t)\boldsymbol{f}(t) depends linearly or nonlinearly on the lhs unknown DOFs 𝝃⁡(t)\boldsymbol{\xi}(t) too. In such cases, eigen decomposition of “pseudo ODEs” can only obtain decoupled lhs operators on 𝒒⁡(t)\boldsymbol{q}(t) on the lhs, but rhs operators on 𝒒⁡(t)\boldsymbol{q}(t) often remain coupled, not only because of the nonlinearity of operators, but also because eigen decomposition applies to the local subsystem but not the global system where rhs sources come from. Hammer-string coupling is a typical example: the string displacement depends on the felt’s force, the felt’s force depends on its compression, but this compression depends on string displacement. Another example is in soundboard-string coupling, the soundboard displacement at the coupling point depends on the string’s surface force, the string’s surface force depends on its displacement, computing its displacement requires knowing the coupling point displacement (Dirichlet boundary), but this displacement depends on the soundboard displacement at the coupling point to satisfy the continuity condition.

An explanation for these seemingly odd relations is that a theoretically sound way would seem to do computations as if all subsystems were a single system, rather than to separate systems and reintroduce coupling between them. This means all DOFs are integrated into a single vector of DOFs, all mass (or stiffness) matrices are assembled into a bigger one, displacements at coupling positions are expressed by the same unique DOFs behind, in order for full coupling solutions. However, this is often unacceptable not only because of the high costs of storage and computation, but also because the inherent heterogeneities of different subsystems, particularly the nonlinearity of hammer felt compression, the first-order characteristic of acoustic system, the different damping mechanisms, may actually not cohere well and may even be tough to control in a single system. Therefore, we shall still adopt the framework of separate systems with mutual coupling, and seek for numeric schemes capable of achieving a level of accuracy as close to full coupling schemes as possible.

The time domain scheme we shall introduce here is inspired by the idea of velocity Verlet algorithms, but customized for our case of modal-transformed first and second order ODEs, with second-order accuracy99 9 Alternatively, one may consider transforming time domain into frequency domain to explore coupling from the perspective of mobility [34].. Despite being lower-order compared to the complex time schemes in [14, 8], our scheme may be more efficient particularly in eliminating the need to invert or solve big or dense matrices at each step, even when the mass matrix is non-diagonal. Due to the existence of coupling, the analytical solutions of first and second order ODEs discussed in section 7.1 may be not applicable here. Nevertheless, system decoupling and dimension reduction via modal decomposition will be shown useful in improving the efficiency of time-stepping algorithms.

7.2.1 Time stepping of second-order ODEs

In the previously derived second-order decoupled ODEs (7.3d), the rhs source term can rewritten as

𝒒¨​(t)+2​μ​𝚲​𝒒˙​(t)+𝚲​𝒒​(t)=𝒑⁡(t),𝒑⁡(t)=𝒓⁡(t,𝒒⁡(t),𝒒˙​(t)),\ddot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t)+2\mu\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t)+\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{q}(t)=\boldsymbol{p}(t),\;\boldsymbol{p}(t)=\boldsymbol{r}\left(t,\boldsymbol{q}(t),\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t)\right), (7.22)

where 𝒓\boldsymbol{r} incoporate all DOF-independent and DOF-dependent contributions to the source term; DOF-dependent contributions consist of two major sources: non-zero Dirichlet boundary conditions; non-conservative force (but excluding damping force already on the lhs).

To perform time discretization, we define the discrete time interval as h=Δ​th=\Delta t, which can be chosen as 1/44100 seconds for producing 44.1 kHz digital audio; define the nn th discrete point in time as tn=n​ht_{n}=nh. The notion of discrete points in time form the basis of time stepping algorithms, where integrations are performed between time steps. An integral over a small interval [x0,x0+Δ​x][x_{0},x_{0}+\Delta x] can be approximated as area of trapeziud

∫x0x0+hf⁡(x)​𝑑x≈h2​[f⁡(x0)+f⁡(x0+h)],\int_{x_{0}}^{x_{0}+h}f(x)\mathrm{d}x\approx\frac{h}{2}\left[f(x_{0})+f(x_{0}+h)\right], (7.23)

which can achieve a relatively high accuracy as per the mean value theorem for definite integrals, though f⁡(x0+h)f(x_{0}+h) may not be known beforehand in some contexts. If we seek for a first-order approximation of f⁡(x0+h)f(x_{0}+h), then

∫x0x0+hf⁡(x)​𝑑x≈h​f​(x0)+h22​f′​(x0)\int_{x_{0}}^{x_{0}+h}f(x)\mathrm{d}x\approx hf(x_{0})+\frac{h^{2}}{2}f^{\prime}(x_{0}) (7.24)

is a less accurate approximation. Utilizing these integration strategies, we integrate (7.22) over [tn,tn+1][t_{n},t_{n+1}] to get

𝒒˙​(tn+1)−𝒒˙​(tn)\displaystyle\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t_{n+1})-\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t_{n}) =−2​μ​𝚲​[𝒒⁡(tn+1)−𝒒⁡(tn)]−s​𝚲​∫tntn+1𝒒⁡(t)​𝑑t+∫tntn+1𝒑⁡(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle=-2\mu\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\left[\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n})\right]-s\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n+1}}\boldsymbol{q}(t)\mathrm{d}t+\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n+1}}\boldsymbol{p}(t)\mathrm{d}t
𝒒˙​(tn+1)−𝒒˙​(tn)\displaystyle\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t_{n+1})-\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t_{n}) ≈−2​μ​𝚲​[𝒒⁡(tn+1)−𝒒⁡(tn)]−h2​𝚲​[𝒒⁡(tn)+𝒒⁡(tn+1)]+h​𝒑​(tn)+h22​𝒑˙​(tn).\displaystyle\approx-2\mu\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\left[\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n})\right]-\frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\left[\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n})+\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n+1})\right]+h\boldsymbol{p}(t_{n})+\frac{h^{2}}{2}\dot{\boldsymbol{p}}(t_{n}). (7.25)

Also it is obvious that

𝒒⁡(tn+1)−𝒒⁡(tn)=∫tntn+1𝒒˙​(t)​𝑑t≈h2​[𝒒˙​(tn)+𝒒˙​(tn+1)].\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n})=\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n+1}}\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t)\mathrm{d}t\approx\frac{h}{2}\left[\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t_{n})+\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t_{n+1})\right]. (7.26)

The solution of (7.25) (7.26) is

𝒒⁡(tn+1)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n+1}) =𝒁1−1​[𝒁0​𝒒​(tn)+2​𝒒˙​(tn)+h​𝒑​(tn)+h22​𝒑˙​(tn)],\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{Z}_{1}^{-1}\left[\boldsymbol{Z}_{0}\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n})+2\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t_{n})+h\boldsymbol{p}(t_{n})+\frac{h^{2}}{2}\dot{\boldsymbol{p}}(t_{n})\right],
𝒒˙​(tn+1)\displaystyle\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t_{n+1}) =2h​𝒒​(tn+1)−2h​𝒒​(tn)−𝒒˙​(tn),\displaystyle=\frac{2}{h}\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n+1})-\frac{2}{h}\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n})-\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t_{n}), (7.27)

where

𝒁0\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Z}_{0} =2h​𝑰+(2​μ−h2)​𝚲,\displaystyle=\frac{2}{h}\boldsymbol{I}+\left(2\mu-\frac{h}{2}\right)\boldsymbol{\Lambda},
𝒁1\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Z}_{1} =2h​𝑰+(2​μ+h2)​𝚲.\displaystyle=\frac{2}{h}\boldsymbol{I}+\left(2\mu+\frac{h}{2}\right)\boldsymbol{\Lambda}. (7.28)

are diagonal matrices easy to invert. (7.27) reveal that 𝒒⁡(tn+1)\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n+1}), 𝒒˙​(tn+1)\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t_{n+1}) can be computed with second-order accuracy using 𝒒⁡(tn)\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n}), 𝒒˙​(tn)\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t_{n}), 𝒑⁡(tn)\boldsymbol{p}(t_{n}), 𝒑˙​(tn)\dot{\boldsymbol{p}}(t_{n}), but without using unknowns of the tn+1t_{n+1} step. This means our time discretization scheme is explicit. As for its energy property, readers can go to appendix D for a detailed deduction incorporating nonlinear strain energy. From the deduction there, our preliminary judgement is that this explicit scheme is energy stable at least for the kinetic energy, potential energy and damping, but uncertain for other non-conservative forces on the rhs. The most significant accuracy loss of this scheme seems to be the use of (7.24) rather than (7.23) in approximating the integral of 𝒑⁡(t)\boldsymbol{p}(t), which may also lead to energy unstability. We would expect the first-order approximation of 𝒑⁡(tn+1)\boldsymbol{p}(t_{n+1}) to be acceptable with small hh. This actually implies that we rely on some historical (tnt_{n}) displacement and velocity values to predict the current (tn+1t_{n+1}) input sources, then the current input sources are updated by the computed current displacement and velocity values. This process can be repeated several times for one time step if higher accuracy and better energy stability is desired, able to use (7.23) rather than (7.24) in approximating the integral of 𝒑⁡(t)\boldsymbol{p}(t).

7.2.2 Time stepping of first-order ODEs

Recall the previously derived first-order decoupled ODEs (7.15b), the rhs source term can rewritten as

𝒒˙​(t)+𝚲​𝒒​(t)=𝒑⁡(t),𝒑⁡(t)=𝒓⁡(t,𝒒⁡(t)),\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}(t)+\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{q}(t)=\boldsymbol{p}(t),\;\boldsymbol{p}(t)=\boldsymbol{r}\left(t,\boldsymbol{q}(t)\right), (7.29)

where 𝒓\boldsymbol{r} incoporate all DOF-independent and DOF-dependent contributions to the source term; DOF-dependent contributions consist of two major sources: non-zero Dirichlet boundary conditions; non-conservative force (but excluding damping force already on the lhs). Integrating (7.29) over [tn,tn+1][t_{n},t_{n+1}], the approximate solution of 𝒒⁡(tn+1)\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n+1}) can be found as

𝒒⁡(tn+1)−𝒒⁡(tn)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n}) =−𝚲∫tntn+1𝒒(t)dt+∫tntn+1𝒑(t)dt\displaystyle=-\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n+1}}\boldsymbol{q}(t)\mathrm{d}t+\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n+1}}\boldsymbol{p}(t)\mathrm{d}t
𝒒⁡(tn+1)−𝒒⁡(tn)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n}) ≈−h2​𝚲​[𝒒⁡(tn)+𝒒⁡(tn+1)]+h​𝒑​(tn)+h22​𝒑˙​(tn)\displaystyle\approx-\frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\left[\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n})+\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n+1})\right]+h\boldsymbol{p}(t_{n})+\frac{h^{2}}{2}\dot{\boldsymbol{p}}(t_{n})
𝒒⁡(tn+1)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n+1}) =(𝑰+h2​𝚲)−1​[(𝑰−h2​𝚲)​𝒒​(tn)+h​𝒑​(tn)+h22​𝒑˙​(tn)].\displaystyle=\left(\boldsymbol{I}+\frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\right)^{-1}\left[\left(\boldsymbol{I}-\frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\right)\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n})+h\boldsymbol{p}(t_{n})+\frac{h^{2}}{2}\dot{\boldsymbol{p}}(t_{n})\right]. (7.30)

Therefore, 𝒒⁡(tn+1)\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n+1}) can be computed using 𝒒⁡(tn)\boldsymbol{q}(t_{n}), 𝒑⁡(tn)\boldsymbol{p}(t_{n}), 𝒑˙​(tn)\dot{\boldsymbol{p}}(t_{n}), but without using unknowns of the tn+1t_{n+1} step.

7.2.3 Time stepping of hammer shank rotation ODE

The equation of hammer shank motion (6.36) can be written in a more abstract way as

I​θ¨=−μ​θ˙+T⁡(θ),I\ddot{\theta}=-\mu\dot{\theta}+T(\theta), (7.31)

where T⁡(θ)T(\theta) incoporate the contributions of gravity and felt force to the total torque of shank, dependent on the zero-order value of θ\theta. Similar to second-order system ODEs, the time discretization of (7.31) is found to be

I⁡[θ˙​(tn+1)−θ˙​(tn)]=−μ⁡[θ⁡(tn+1)−θ⁡(tn)]+∫tntn+1T⁡(θ)​𝑑t\displaystyle I\left[\dot{\theta}(t_{n+1})-\dot{\theta}(t_{n})\right]=-\mu\left[\theta(t_{n+1})-\theta(t_{n})\right]+\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n+1}}T(\theta)\mathrm{d}t
I⁡[2h​θ​(tn+1)−2h​θ​(tn)−2​θ˙​(tn)]≈−μ⁡[θ⁡(tn+1)−θ⁡(tn)]+h​T​(tn)+h22​T˙​(tn)\displaystyle I\left[\frac{2}{h}\theta(t_{n+1})-\frac{2}{h}\theta(t_{n})-2\dot{\theta}(t_{n})\right]\approx-\mu\left[\theta(t_{n+1})-\theta(t_{n})\right]+hT(t_{n})+\frac{h^{2}}{2}\dot{T}(t_{n})
θ⁡(tn+1)=(2h​I+μ)−1​[(2h​I+μ)​θ​(tn)+2​θ˙​(tn)+h​T​(tn)+h22​T˙​(tn)],\displaystyle\theta(t_{n+1})=\left(\frac{2}{h}I+\mu\right)^{-1}\left[\left(\frac{2}{h}I+\mu\right)\theta(t_{n})+2\dot{\theta}(t_{n})+hT(t_{n})+\frac{h^{2}}{2}\dot{T}(t_{n})\right], (7.32)

and

θ˙​(tn+1)=2h​θ​(tn+1)−2h​θ​(tn)−θ˙​(tn).\dot{\theta}(t_{n+1})=\frac{2}{h}\theta(t_{n+1})-\frac{2}{h}\theta(t_{n})-\dot{\theta}(t_{n}). (7.33)

Therefore, θ⁡(tn+1)\theta(t_{n+1}) and θ˙​(tn+1)\dot{\theta}(t_{n+1}) can be computed using θ⁡(tn)\theta(t_{n}), θ˙​(tn)\dot{\theta}(t_{n}), T⁡(tn)T(t_{n}), T˙​(tn)\dot{T}(t_{n}), but without using unknowns of the tn+1t_{n+1} step.

7.3 Concatenating the whole model

With modal transformation and time discretization of the ODEs established, it now suffices to combine all parts of the piano model together. The whole computation process consists of two major separate parts: first do space discretization, then do time discretization. Rooted in the time-space separation idea of FEM, these two numeric works do not interfere so computation costs should be acceptable.

  13. 13.

    Compute the next modal DOFs of room barriers using scheme 2a:

    𝒒(f)​(tn),𝒒˙(f)​(tn),𝒑(f)​(tn),𝒑(f)​(tn+1)→𝒒(f)​(tn+1),𝒒˙(f)​(tn+1)\boldsymbol{q}^{(f)}(t_{n}),\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}^{(f)}(t_{n}),\boldsymbol{p}^{(f)}(t_{n}),\boldsymbol{p}^{(f)}(t_{n+1})\rightarrow\boldsymbol{q}^{(f)}(t_{n+1}),\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}^{(f)}(t_{n+1})
  14. 14.

    Compute the next modal forces of air (non-zero boundary condition) using (6.48):

    𝒒(f)​(tn+1),𝒒˙(f)​(tn+1)→𝒑2(c)​(tn+1),𝒑˙2(c)​(tn+1)\boldsymbol{q}^{(f)}(t_{n+1}),\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}^{(f)}(t_{n+1})\rightarrow\boldsymbol{p}_{2}^{(c)}(t_{n+1}),\dot{\boldsymbol{p}}_{2}^{(c)}(t_{n+1})
  15. 15.

    If higher accuracy and better energy stability is desired, repeat the above steps 1 to 14 several times. Note that different from the first iteration, the subsequent iterations always use schemes 1a, 2a, 3a and do not need to use schemes 1b, 2b, 3b. If no more repetition is needed, end the current time step and move on to the next time step.

Audio output

Compute the acoustic pressure signals at certaining listening positions using the stored modal DOFs 𝒒(c)​(tn)​(n=0,…,n1)\boldsymbol{q}^{(c)}(t_{n})\;(n=0,...,n_{1}) and modal superposition. These signals are the final output digital audio of piano simulation model.

8 Conclusion

This paper presented a detailed physical model for simulating acoustic piano sounds. For solid parts of the piano system, viz. strings, soundboard, room barriers, hammer felt, a 3D prestressed elasticity model is generally applied. For fluid parts of the piano system, viz. sound radiation in the air, conservation of mass and Navier-Stokes equation is applied. For coupling between different subsystems of the piano, mechanisms of surface force transmission and displacement/velocity continuity are considered. For numeric simulation, modal superposition and explicit time discretization schemes are utilized. Despite the complexity of this whole piano model, we have paid efforts to a straightforward presentation based more on system ODEs transformed from strong PDEs, as well as a time domain simulation scheme balancing efficiency and accuracy.

Below discusses the current study’s limitations and our plans or recommendations for future research.

  • •

    Waiting for numeric simulation results. Due to the complication of our piano model, we choose to write down theoretic models first as a guiding framework. Our next step involves implementing the computation procedures using high-performance, expressive and well-structured programming languages like Rust, as well as performing result analysis using convenient and ecologically rich programming languages like Python. Facing some unknown uncertainties in practice, our model needs to be further tested and improved.

  • •

    In hammer felt-string coupling and string-soundboard coupling, the contact was treated as occuring at a point rather than an area. This simplification would probably lead to a loss in realism. The 3D contact framework described in appendix C may apply here, but algorithmic complexity and numeric stability needs to be better addressed.

  • •

    The string-soundboard coupling mechanism was assumed of fixation but not collision nature. A coupling model similar to the nonlinear hammer-string interaction may be more suitable, considering that a string seems to actually be supported between two distanced bridge pins. The 3D contact framework described in appendix C may apply here, but algorithmic complexity and numeric stability needs to be better addressed. It also remains to discover how the relative positions of the two pins affect the vibrations of the string and soundboard.

  • •

    Treatment of nonlinear coupling between the distinct subsystems of the piano in time discretization schemes remains challenging. As far as we understand, only nonlinear implicit schemes can achieve unconditional energy stability if the two coupling mechanisms we consider, namely the surface force transmission and the displacement/velocity continuity, exhibit nonlinearity. A viable tradeoff between accuracy and efficiency may be the explicit iteration approach we proposed, but we hope to see better alternatives.

  • •

    The damping in our model is relatively simplified, as only one or two viscousity coefficients are used. It may be beneficial to introduce additional unknowns like temperature and additional governing equations like thermal equations to reflect the damping phenomena more realistically.

  • •

    Some observed phenomena of acoustic pianos are still missing their representations in our model. For example, strings not striked by the hammer may also vibrate as long as the sustain pedal is pressed, which is often called sympathetic resonance. An explanation for this is that the striked string transmits its vibration to other strings through the variation of air pressure, which can actually lead to a string-air coupling model. Also, the transmission of piano player’s key action into hammer shank movement requires further investigation.

  • •

    It remains to discover the relation between physical parameters of the piano model and the objective (waveforms, spectrums) and subjective (listener feel) aspects of the final ouput sound, so that these parameters can be tuned to approach realism or even obtain new sounds without a real world couterpart.

Finally, we hope this study could contribute to the understanding of the vibroacoustics of a piano, and to the innovation of digital musical instruments with desired characteristics of sound.

Appendix A Prestrain and prestress

Consider 3 configurations of a material: natural → initial → current [28]. In the natural configuration, no prestrain and prestress is present. In the initial configuration, prestrain and prestress exist. In the current configuration, strain and stress emerge in addition to prestrain and prestress. Under the same x​y​zxyz coordinate system, define ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} vectors 𝒙¯\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}, 𝒙\boldsymbol{x}, 𝒙^\hat{\boldsymbol{x}} as the coordinates of the same material particle in the natural, initial and current configurations respectively. The following relation holds:

𝒙\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x} =𝒙¯+𝒖¯​(𝒙¯),\displaystyle=\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}+\bar{\boldsymbol{u}}(\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}),
𝒙^\displaystyle\hat{\boldsymbol{x}} =𝒙+𝒖⁡(𝒙),\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}), (A.1)

where 𝒖¯\bar{\boldsymbol{u}} and 𝒖\boldsymbol{u} are the displacement vectors from natural to initial and from initial to current configurations respectively. Denote deformation gradients 𝒁^=∂𝒙^∂𝒙¯\hat{\boldsymbol{Z}}=\frac{\partial\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\partial\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}}, 𝒁=∂𝒙^∂𝒙\boldsymbol{Z}=\frac{\partial\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\partial\boldsymbol{x}} and 𝒁¯=∂𝒙∂𝒙¯\bar{\boldsymbol{Z}}=\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{x}}{\partial\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}}; denote Jacobian matrices 𝑱=∇𝒖\boldsymbol{J}=\nabla\boldsymbol{u}, 𝑱¯=∇𝒖¯\bar{\boldsymbol{J}}=\nabla\bar{\boldsymbol{u}},. We then have

𝒁=𝑰+𝑱,𝒁¯=𝑰+𝑱¯,\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Z}=\boldsymbol{I}+\boldsymbol{J},\;\bar{\boldsymbol{Z}}=\boldsymbol{I}+\bar{\boldsymbol{J}},
𝒁^=𝒁​𝒁¯=(𝑰+𝑱)​(𝑰+𝑱¯).\displaystyle\hat{\boldsymbol{Z}}=\boldsymbol{Z}\bar{\boldsymbol{Z}}=\left(\boldsymbol{I}+\boldsymbol{J}\right)\left(\boldsymbol{I}+\bar{\boldsymbol{J}}\right). (A.2)

The Green-Lagrange strain tensor of current configuration with respect to natural configuration is

≈𝑬~=ϵ+𝑬¯+(𝑱¯⊤​ϵ+ϵ​𝑱¯+𝑱¯⊤​ϵ​𝑱¯),\displaystyle\approx\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}=\boldsymbol{\epsilon}+\bar{\boldsymbol{E}}+\left(\bar{\boldsymbol{J}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\bar{\boldsymbol{J}}+\bar{\boldsymbol{J}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\bar{\boldsymbol{J}}\right), (A.3)

From (A.1), an inverse mapping 𝒙¯=f⁡(𝒙)\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}=f(\boldsymbol{x}) should exist. If we let 𝑻→​(𝒙)=𝑺¯→​(f​(𝒙))\overrightarrow{\boldsymbol{T}}(\boldsymbol{x})=\overrightarrow{\bar{\boldsymbol{S}}}(f(\boldsymbol{x})), the vectorized tension field from (2.8), and subsititute 𝑬¯→=𝑫−1​𝑻→​(𝒙)\overrightarrow{\bar{\boldsymbol{E}}}=\boldsymbol{D}^{-1}\overrightarrow{\boldsymbol{T}}(\boldsymbol{x}) into (A)(A.16), then the total strain 𝑬^\hat{\boldsymbol{E}} can be expressed in only the initial configurations.
