Given the strain vector 𝑬^→\overrightarrow{\hat{\boldsymbol{E}}}, the dynamic strain energy is

U\displaystyle U =∫Ω∫𝟎𝑬~→dynΨ0​𝑺~→dyn⋅d​𝑬~→dyn​𝑑V\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\int_{\boldsymbol{0}}^{\overrightarrow{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}}_{\mathrm{dyn}}}\Psi_{0}\overrightarrow{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{S}}}_{\mathrm{dyn}}\cdot\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}}_{\mathrm{dyn}}\mathrm{d}V
=∫Ω∫𝟎𝑬~→dynΨ0​𝑫​𝑬~→dyn⋅d​𝑬~→dyn​𝑑V\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\int_{\boldsymbol{0}}^{\overrightarrow{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}}_{\mathrm{dyn}}}\Psi_{0}\boldsymbol{D}\overrightarrow{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}}_{\mathrm{dyn}}\cdot\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}}_{\mathrm{dyn}}\mathrm{d}V
=12​∫ΩΨ0​𝑬~→dyn⋅𝑫​𝑬~→dyn​𝑑V\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}\Psi_{0}\overrightarrow{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}}_{\mathrm{dyn}}\cdot\boldsymbol{D}\overrightarrow{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}}_{\mathrm{dyn}}\mathrm{d}V
=∫Ω12​Ψ0​ϵ→⋅(𝑫+𝚿1⊤​𝚿2⊤​𝑫​𝚿2​𝚿1)​ϵ→​𝑑V,\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\frac{1}{2}\Psi_{0}\overrightarrow{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\cdot\left(\boldsymbol{D}+\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{2}^{\top}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{2}\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{1}\right)\overrightarrow{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\mathrm{d}V, (A.17)

where Ψ0​(𝒙)=det(𝒁¯)−1\Psi_{0}(\boldsymbol{x})=\det(\bar{\boldsymbol{Z}})^{-1} is the volume factor linear w.r.t. the unknowns, accounts for volume change from natural to current configuration, and can be computed given 𝑱¯\bar{\boldsymbol{J}}. Note that 𝑺~→dyn\overrightarrow{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{S}}}_{\mathrm{dyn}} here is understood as the (dynamic) second Piola-Kirchhoff (PK2) stress that is energy conjugate to 𝑬~→dyn\overrightarrow{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}}_{\mathrm{dyn}}. Though PK2 should be formulated in the natural configuration, we have transformed it to the initial configuration along with the volume factor. According to [2], PK2 may also be changed to Cauchy stress in the initial configuration, but it is unnecessary here because the strain energy is the same even without doing so. And anyway, what we seek for here is not PK2, but the dynamic stress vector 𝝈→\overrightarrow{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} that is energy conjugate to ϵ→\overrightarrow{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}, which can be derived from the expression of dynamic strain energy as

𝝈^→=(𝑫​ϵ→+𝝉→),𝝉→+Ψ0​𝚿1⊤​𝚿2⊤​𝑫​𝚿2​𝚿1​ϵ→,\overrightarrow{\hat{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}}=\left(\boldsymbol{D}\overrightarrow{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}+\overrightarrow{\boldsymbol{\tau}}\right),\;\overrightarrow{\boldsymbol{\tau}}+\Psi_{0}\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{2}^{\top}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{2}\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{1}\overrightarrow{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}, (A.18)

where 𝝉→\overrightarrow{\boldsymbol{\tau}} is the dynamic prestress vector. It is now clear that the effect of prestress can be seen as adding a symmetrically transformed constitutive matrix 𝚿1⊤​𝚿2⊤​𝑫​𝚿2​𝚿1\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{2}^{\top}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{2}\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{1}.

Finally, we acknowledge that tn the presence of large deformations from initial to current configuration, the quadratic term in the Green-Lagrange strain should be retained, leading to nonlinear operators on the unknowns for the strain energy, as well as PDEs and ODEs. However, this concern is irrelevant in case of large deformations from natural to initial configuration because even if prestrain itself is nonlinear, it is linear w.r.t. the strain where the unknowns are contained in. Another more intricate nonlinearity, often known as the geometric nonlinearity, arises if we want to express stress and prestress in the current configuration. This would require transforming PK2 to Cauchy stress, yet we have not encountered the necessity for doing so in the present context.

Appendix B Lagrangian formulation

As a complement to the Newtonian formulation, we present a non-conservative Lagrangian formulation of the 3D elastic material model. To derive system ODEs (weak form) in a more straightforward way, FEM space discretization is incorporated into the Lagrangian formulation, skipping the intermediate PDEs (strong form). As per (2.2), the kinetic energy and its variation over [t0,t1][t_{0},t_{1}] are

Ek\displaystyle E_{k} =∫Ω12​ρ​𝒖˙⋅𝒖˙​𝑑V=12​∫Ω𝝃˙⋅ρ​𝑷⊤​𝑷​𝝃˙​𝑑V\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\frac{1}{2}\rho\dot{\boldsymbol{u}}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{u}}\mathrm{d}V=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\cdot\rho\boldsymbol{P}^{\top}\boldsymbol{P}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\mathrm{d}V
∫t0t1δ​Ek​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\delta E_{k}\mathrm{d}t =∫t0t1∫Ωδ𝝃˙⋅ρ𝑷⊤𝑷𝝃˙dVdt=−∫t0t1∫Ωδ𝝃⋅ρ𝑷⊤𝑷𝝃¨dVdt\displaystyle=\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\int_{\Omega}\delta\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\cdot\rho\boldsymbol{P}^{\top}\boldsymbol{P}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\mathrm{d}V\mathrm{d}t=-\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\int_{\Omega}\delta\boldsymbol{\xi}\cdot\rho\boldsymbol{P}^{\top}\boldsymbol{P}\ddot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\mathrm{d}V\mathrm{d}t (B.1)

where integration by parts is utilized assuming

δ​𝝃​(t0)=δ​𝝃​(t1)=𝟎.\delta\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{0})=\delta\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{1})=\boldsymbol{0}. (B.2)

Note that we have excluded 𝝃0\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0} in the derivation of kinetic energy because nonzero 𝝃0\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0} (boundary displacements) actually implys the existence some non-conservative forces (e.g. constraints). Nevertheless, we can compute the “virtual kinetic energy” as

∫t0t1δ​Ek,0=∫t0t1∫Ωδ​𝝃˙⋅ρ​𝑷⊤​𝑷0​𝝃˙0​𝑑V​𝑑t\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\delta E_{k,0}=\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\int_{\Omega}\delta\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\cdot\rho\boldsymbol{P}^{\top}\boldsymbol{P}_{0}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_{0}\mathrm{d}V\mathrm{d}t (B.3)

The potential energy and its variation are

Ep\displaystyle E_{p} =−∫Ω12𝒖⋅Div(𝝈+𝝉)dV\displaystyle=-\int_{\Omega}\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{u}\cdot\mathrm{Div}\left(\boldsymbol{\sigma}+\boldsymbol{\tau}\right)\mathrm{d}V
=−∫Γ(12∑i=13ui(𝝈i+𝝉i))⋅d𝚪+∫Ω(12∑i=13∇ui⋅(𝝈i+𝝉i))dV\displaystyle=-\int_{\Gamma}\left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{3}u_{i}\left(\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{i}+\boldsymbol{\tau}_{i}\right)\right)\cdot\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}+\int_{\Omega}\left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{3}\nabla u_{i}\cdot\left(\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{i}+\boldsymbol{\tau}_{i}\right)\right)\mathrm{d}V
=∫Ω[∑i=1312​(𝝃⋅𝑸i⊤​(𝑨i+𝑩i)​𝑸​𝝃)]​𝑑V\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{3}\frac{1}{2}\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\cdot\boldsymbol{Q}_{i}^{\top}\left(\boldsymbol{A}_{i}+\boldsymbol{B}_{i}\right)\boldsymbol{Q}\boldsymbol{\xi}\right)\right]\mathrm{d}V
=∫Ω12​𝝃⋅𝑸⊤​(𝑨+𝑩)​𝑸​𝝃​𝑑V\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\xi}\cdot\boldsymbol{Q}^{\top}\left(\boldsymbol{A}+\boldsymbol{B}\right)\boldsymbol{Q}\boldsymbol{\xi}\mathrm{d}V
δ​Ep\displaystyle\delta E_{p} =∫Ωδ​𝝃⋅𝑸⊤​(𝑨+𝑩)​𝑸​𝝃​𝑑V\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\delta\boldsymbol{\xi}\cdot\boldsymbol{Q}^{\top}\left(\boldsymbol{A}+\boldsymbol{B}\right)\boldsymbol{Q}\boldsymbol{\xi}\mathrm{d}V (B.4)

where Dirichlet or Neumann boundary conditions should automatically apply to ensure the integral on the boundary is zero. Similar to the kinetic energy, nonzero 𝝃0\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0} does not correspond to a potential energy but a “virtual potential energy” (equivalent to virtual work but sign flipped here for convenience) as

δ​Ep,0=∫Ωδ​𝝃⋅𝑸⊤​(𝑨+𝑩)​𝑸0​𝝃0​𝑑V\delta E_{p,0}=\int_{\Omega}\delta\boldsymbol{\xi}\cdot\boldsymbol{Q}^{\top}\left(\boldsymbol{A}+\boldsymbol{B}\right)\boldsymbol{Q}_{0}\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0}\mathrm{d}V (B.5)

As for the damping force which is non-conservative, we can compute its virtual work as

δ​Wd\displaystyle\delta W_{d} =2​μ​∫Ωδ​𝒖⋅Div⁡(𝝈˙+𝝉˙)​𝑑V\displaystyle=2\mu\int_{\Omega}\delta\boldsymbol{u}\cdot\mathrm{Div}\left(\dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}+\dot{\boldsymbol{\tau}}\right)\mathrm{d}V
=−2μ∫Ω[∑i=13δ∇ui⋅(𝝈˙i+𝝉˙i)]dV\displaystyle=-2\mu\int_{\Omega}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{3}\delta\nabla u_{i}\cdot\left(\dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{i}+\dot{\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{i}\right)\right]\mathrm{d}V
=−2μ∫Ωδ𝝃⋅[𝑸⊤(𝑨+𝑩)𝑸𝝃˙+𝑸⊤(𝑨+𝑩)𝑸0𝝃0˙]dV.\displaystyle=-2\mu\int_{\Omega}\delta\boldsymbol{\xi}\cdot\left[\boldsymbol{Q}^{\top}\left(\boldsymbol{A}+\boldsymbol{B}\right)\boldsymbol{Q}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}+\boldsymbol{Q}^{\top}\left(\boldsymbol{A}+\boldsymbol{B}\right)\boldsymbol{Q}_{0}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0}}\right]\mathrm{d}V. (B.6)

It can be verified that the virtual work approach is also applicable to conservative forces like stress and prestress to derive the identical potential energy functions. For other non-conservative forces, the virtual work is

δ​Wn​c=∫Ωδ​𝒖⋅𝑭​𝑑V=∫Ωδ​𝝃⋅𝑷⊤​𝑭​𝑑V.\delta W_{nc}=\int_{\Omega}\delta\boldsymbol{u}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}\mathrm{d}V=\int_{\Omega}\delta\boldsymbol{\xi}\cdot\boldsymbol{P}^{\top}\boldsymbol{F}\mathrm{d}V. (B.7)

Applying the principle of virtual work, we derive the energy equation

∫t0t1(δEk+δEk,0−δEp−δEp,0+δWd+δWn​c)dt=−∫t0t1δ𝝃⋅(𝑴𝝃¨+𝑪𝝃˙+𝑲𝝃−𝒇)dt=0,\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\left(\delta E_{k}+\delta E_{k,0}-\delta E_{p}-\delta E_{p,0}+\delta W_{d}+\delta W_{nc}\right)\mathrm{d}t=-\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\delta\boldsymbol{\xi}\cdot\left(\boldsymbol{M}\ddot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}+\boldsymbol{C}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}+\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{\xi}-\boldsymbol{f}\right)\mathrm{d}t=0, (B.8)

where 𝑴\boldsymbol{M}, 𝑪\boldsymbol{C}, 𝑲\boldsymbol{K}, 𝒇\boldsymbol{f} are defined in (2.43). Since δ​𝝃\delta\boldsymbol{\xi} is arbitrary as long as (B.2) is satisfied, (2.42) can be derived from (B.8).

Appendix C Elastic material contacting rigid surface in 3D setting

We now consider the case of a material A contacting another material B in a fully 3D setting, where A is elastic with weak form ODEs like (2.42) and B’s contact surface is rigid (hence B may still be an elastic material). In this case, applying Dirichlet boundary conditions through 𝝃0​(t)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0}(t) would be infeasible because not only the contact status (in contact or not) but also the contact boundary changes with time. As we shall see, the potential contact boundary is Dirichlet when contact is present meaning that boundary stress and strain appear, and is Neumann when contact is absent meaning that boundary stress and strain vanish. This leads to a time-varying dimension (number of DOFs) of the system ODEs, invalidating the modal superposition method. To model the dynamic evolution of contact system, we adopt the master-slave idea and will brief describe our understanding and application of it. Readers can refer to [37][24] for a comprehensive and rigorous FEM formulation of the contact problem.

Consider a system of second-order ODEs where the rhs source term depends on the DOFs:

𝑴​𝝃¨​(t)+𝑪​𝝃˙​(t)+𝑲​𝝃​(t)=𝒇⁡(t),𝒇⁡(t)=𝒓⁡(t,𝝃⁡(t),𝝃˙​(t)).\boldsymbol{M}\ddot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)+\boldsymbol{C}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)+\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)=\boldsymbol{f}(t),\;\boldsymbol{f}(t)=\boldsymbol{r}\left(t,\boldsymbol{\xi}(t),\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)\right). (C.1)

To derive time stepping algorithms like those in 7.2, we first integrate (C.1) over [tn,tn+1][t_{n},t_{n+1}] to yield

𝑴⁡[𝝃˙​(tn+1)−𝝃˙​(tn)]\displaystyle\boldsymbol{M}\left[\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n+1})-\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n})\right] =−𝑪⁡[𝝃⁡(tn+1)−𝝃⁡(tn)]−𝑲​∫tntn+1𝝃⁡(t)​𝑑t+∫tntn+1𝒇⁡(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle=-\boldsymbol{C}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})\right]-\boldsymbol{K}\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n+1}}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\mathrm{d}t+\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n+1}}\boldsymbol{f}(t)\mathrm{d}t
𝑴⁡[𝝃˙​(tn+1)−𝝃˙​(tn)]\displaystyle\boldsymbol{M}\left[\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n+1})-\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n})\right] ≈−𝑪⁡[𝝃⁡(tn+1)−𝝃⁡(tn)]−h2​𝑲​[𝝃⁡(tn)+𝝃⁡(tn+1)]+h​𝒇​(tn)+h22​𝒇˙​(tn).\displaystyle\approx-\boldsymbol{C}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})\right]-\frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{K}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})+\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})\right]+h\boldsymbol{f}(t_{n})+\frac{h^{2}}{2}\dot{\boldsymbol{f}}(t_{n}). (C.2)

Combining this with

𝝃⁡(tn+1)−𝝃⁡(tn)=∫tntn+1𝝃˙​(t)​𝑑t≈h2​[𝝃˙​(tn)+𝝃˙​(tn+1)],\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})=\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n+1}}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)\mathrm{d}t\approx\frac{h}{2}\left[\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n})+\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n+1})\right], (C.3)

the update scheme for DOFs vector is found to be

𝝃⁡(tn+1)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1}) =𝒁1−1​[𝒁0​𝝃​(tn)+2​𝑴​𝝃˙​(tn)+h​𝒇​(tn)+h22​𝒇˙​(tn)],\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{Z}_{1}^{-1}\left[\boldsymbol{Z}_{0}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})+2\boldsymbol{M}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n})+h\boldsymbol{f}(t_{n})+\frac{h^{2}}{2}\dot{\boldsymbol{f}}(t_{n})\right],
𝝃˙​(tn+1)\displaystyle\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n+1}) =2h​𝝃​(tn+1)−2h​𝝃​(tn)−𝝃˙​(tn),\displaystyle=\frac{2}{h}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\frac{2}{h}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})-\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n}), (C.4)

where

𝒁0\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Z}_{0} =2h​𝑴+𝑪−h2​𝑲,\displaystyle=\frac{2}{h}\boldsymbol{M}+\boldsymbol{C}-\frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{K},
𝒁1\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Z}_{1} =2h​𝑴+𝑪+h2​𝑲.\displaystyle=\frac{2}{h}\boldsymbol{M}+\boldsymbol{C}+\frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{K}. (C.5)

It now suffices to describe the time stepping algorithm for contact problem as follows:

Here we assume the rhs source only comes from contact between A and B. If any other rhs sources are present and independent of this contact, add them to 𝒇ja​(tn)\boldsymbol{f}_{j}^{a}(t_{n}) and 𝒇ja˙​(tn)\dot{\boldsymbol{f}_{j}^{a}}(t_{n}).

    Input 𝝃ja​(tn)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a}(t_{n}), 𝝃ja˙​(tn)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a}}(t_{n}), 𝒇ja​(tn)\boldsymbol{f}_{j}^{a}(t_{n}), 𝒇ja˙​(tn)\dot{\boldsymbol{f}_{j}^{a}}(t_{n}), 𝑴ja\boldsymbol{M}_{j}^{a}, 𝑪ja\boldsymbol{C}_{j}^{a}, 𝑲ja\boldsymbol{K}_{j}^{a} into (C.4) to compute 𝝃ja​(tn+1)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a}(t_{n+1}) and 𝝃ja˙​(tn+1)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a}}(t_{n+1}).

Here 𝝃ja​(tn+1)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a}(t_{n+1}) and 𝝃ja˙​(tn+1)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a}}(t_{n+1}) are used to compute A’s surface forces acting on B, so as to obtain B’s displacements at tn+1t_{n+1}.

Note here 𝝃j−1b​(tn)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j-1}^{b}(t_{n}), 𝝃j−1b˙​(tn)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j-1}^{b}}(t_{n}) (if any) must be classified as penetrated in 𝝃jb​(tn)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{b}(t_{n}), 𝝃jb˙​(tn)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{b}}(t_{n}). Accordingly, 𝑴\boldsymbol{M}, 𝑪\boldsymbol{C}, 𝑲\boldsymbol{K} are adjusted to 𝑴ja\boldsymbol{M}_{j}^{a}, 𝑪ja\boldsymbol{C}_{j}^{a}, 𝑲ja\boldsymbol{K}_{j}^{a} with dimension NjaN_{j}^{a}, in a way as if 𝝃ja\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a} were 𝝃\boldsymbol{\xi} (unknown DOFs) and 𝝃jb\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{b} were 𝝃0\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0} (known DOFs) in (2.43). Using 𝝃jb​(tn)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{b}(t_{n}) and 𝝃jb˙​(tn)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{b}}(t_{n}) (Dirichlet boundary conditions), 𝒇ja​(tn)\boldsymbol{f}_{j}^{a}(t_{n}) and 𝒇ja˙​(tn)\dot{\boldsymbol{f}_{j}^{a}}(t_{n}) with dimension NjaN_{j}^{a} can be computed.

        Input 𝝃ja​(tn)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a}(t_{n}), 𝝃ja˙​(tn)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a}}(t_{n}), 𝒇ja​(tn)\boldsymbol{f}_{j}^{a}(t_{n}), 𝒇ja˙​(tn)\dot{\boldsymbol{f}_{j}^{a}}(t_{n}), 𝑴ja\boldsymbol{M}_{j}^{a}, 𝑪ja\boldsymbol{C}_{j}^{a}, 𝑲ja\boldsymbol{K}_{j}^{a} into (C.4) to compute 𝝃ja​(tn+1)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a}(t_{n+1}) and 𝝃ja˙​(tn+1)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a}}(t_{n+1}).

      3. iii.

        Based on 𝝃ja​(tn+1)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a}(t_{n+1}) and 𝝃ja˙​(tn+1)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a}}(t_{n+1}), check if A “penetrates” B at any potential contact boundary nodes using a geometry searching algorithm. Here 𝝃ja​(tn+1)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a}(t_{n+1}) and 𝝃ja˙​(tn+1)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a}}(t_{n+1}) are used to compute A’s surface forces acting on B, so as to obtain B’s displacements at tn+1t_{n+1}, as well as 𝝃jb​(tn+1)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{b}(t_{n+1}) and 𝝃jb˙​(tn+1)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{b}}(t_{n+1}). Note here if 𝝃jb˙​(tn+1)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{b}}(t_{n+1}) is not well-defined due to non-smoothness, the weak derivative may be adopted as an alternative. Combine 𝝃ja​(tn+1)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a}(t_{n+1}), 𝝃ja˙​(tn+1)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a}}(t_{n+1}) and 𝝃jb​(tn+1)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{b}(t_{n+1}), 𝝃jb˙​(tn+1)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{b}}(t_{n+1}) to get 𝝃j​(tn+1)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}(t_{n+1}) and 𝝃˙j​(tn+1)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_{j}(t_{n+1}).

        1. A.

          If penetration occurs at some nodes, go back to step 3.(a).i.

        2. B.

          Otherwise, go to step 4.

    2. (b)

      Otherwise, set 𝝃j​(tn+1)=𝝃ja​(tn+1)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}(t_{n+1})=\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a}(t_{n+1}), 𝝃˙j​(tn+1)=𝝃ja˙​(tn+1)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_{j}(t_{n+1})=\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{a}}(t_{n+1}).

  4. 4.

    End the current time step with 𝝃⁡(tn+1)=𝝃j​(tn+1)\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})=\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}(t_{n+1}) and 𝝃˙​(tn+1)=𝝃˙j​(tn+1)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n+1})=\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_{j}(t_{n+1}), and move on to the next time step.

The basic idea of this algorithm is to try Neumann first, and if penetration occurs then change to Dirichlet. This strategy can be justified from an energy perspective: first seek for displacements minimizing the Lagrangian and virtual work of the system without any constraint; if unrealistic penetration occurs, add an equality constraint regarding Dirichlet boundary displacements, so as to find displacements minimizing the Lagrangian and virtual work under contact constraint (similar to the Lagrange multipliers). This check of penetration can lead to the nonlinearity and non-smoothness of a contact problem. For geometry searching algorithms needed to check penetration, we refer to the [COMSOL description]. If the contact boundary is assumed to be only a fixed point, then only one or two iterations per time step is needed.

Certain contact problems may involve deformations large enough to induce non-negligible nonlinearity. For nonlinearity of strain, the Green-Lagrange strain instead of the engineering strain may be needed. For nonlinearity of stress, the second-Piola–Kirchhoff stress tensor instead of the Cauchy stress tensor may be needed. This would introduce another kind of nonlinearity into the contact model. While the nonlinearity due to contact’s one-sided nature still keeps the computation of each iteration in one time step linear, the nonlinearity due to nonlinear stress and strain can make the PDEs as well as ODEs nonlinear, meaning that computation of each iteration is nonlinear if no linearization is applied. If the nonlinear perturbation to the equations is small (controlled by some “small parameters”), the perturbation method applying linearization several times is acceptable; otherwise, the perturbation method would suffer significant accuracy loss.

Appendix D An energy-stable scheme for nonlinear forces

To better solve elastic solid problems subject to deformation nonlinearity, particularly elastic contact and piano string vibration, we are working on integrating into our model the invariant energy quadratization (IEQ) method [38] and scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) method [29, 30]. Based on the idea of IEQ, SAV is a recent advancement in computational physics towards efficient and energy-stable time discretization scheme for gradient flows. Both methods have been applied to musical instruments modeling, achieving discrete energy evolution (conservation or dissipation) that is consistent with the continuous counterpart, using fully explicit or linearly implicit update schemes [18, 36, 6]. These schemes attain the desired discrete energy-stable property while being more efficient than existing nonlinear solvers many of which rely on Newton-Raphson like iterations with computationally expensive Jacobian matrices.

To introduce nonlinearity into the 3D elastic solid model, we rewrite (2.42) as

𝑴​𝝃¨​(t)+𝑪​𝝃˙​(t)+𝑲​𝝃​(t)+𝒈⁡[𝝃⁡(t)]=𝒇⁡(t),\boldsymbol{M}\ddot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)+\boldsymbol{C}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)+\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)+\boldsymbol{g}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right]=\boldsymbol{f}(t), (D.1)

where 𝒈⁡(𝝃)\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) is an operator incorporating all the “symmetric” nonlinear forces of the system, which can be conservative or non-conservative. The symmetry property we require here means that 𝒈\boldsymbol{g} is a self-adjoint operator thus the variational Jacobian matrix

𝑱⁡[𝝃⁡(t)]=δ𝝃​𝒈\boldsymbol{J}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right]=\delta_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\boldsymbol{g} (D.2)

is symmetric. This is equivalent to 𝒈\boldsymbol{g} being a self-adjoint operator. For simplicity we have not considered nonlinear damping forces in the form of 𝒈1​(𝝃˙)\boldsymbol{g}_{1}(\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}) here, but they can simply be treated in a similar way to 𝒈⁡(𝝃)\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{\xi}). An example of nonlinear symmetric forces is the nonlinear stress arising from the quadratic term in Green-Lagrange strain, as well as the damping force proportional to its first-order time derivative. Anyway, linear or nonlinear forces not satisfying this symmetry property are incorporated in 𝒇⁡(t)\boldsymbol{f}(t), and unfortunately the coupling forces in our piano model are probably such examples. The symmetry property has important implications that one can define a nonlinear energy functional as

En​l​[𝝃⁡(t)]=∫0t𝝃˙​(t′)⋅𝒈⁡[𝝃⁡(t′)]​d​t′,E_{nl}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right]=\int_{0}^{t}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t^{\prime})\cdot\boldsymbol{g}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t^{\prime})\right]\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}, (D.3)

with first-order time derivative

∂tEn​l​[𝝃⁡(t)]=𝝃˙​(t)⋅𝒈⁡[𝝃⁡(t)],\partial_{t}E_{nl}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right]=\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)\cdot\boldsymbol{g}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right], (D.4)

and variation

δ​En​l​[𝝃⁡(t)]\displaystyle\delta E_{nl}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right] =∫0tδ​𝝃˙⋅𝒈​d​t′+∫0t𝝃˙⋅δ​𝒈​d​t′,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{t}\delta\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\cdot\boldsymbol{g}\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}+\int_{0}^{t}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\cdot\delta\boldsymbol{g}\mathrm{d}t^{\prime},
=δ​𝝃​(t)⋅𝒈−δ​𝝃​(0)⋅𝒈+∫0t𝝃˙⋅δ​𝒈​d​t′−∫0tδ​𝝃⋅𝒈˙​d​t′\displaystyle=\delta\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\cdot\boldsymbol{g}-\delta\boldsymbol{\xi}(0)\cdot\boldsymbol{g}+\int_{0}^{t}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\cdot\delta\boldsymbol{g}\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}-\int_{0}^{t}\delta\boldsymbol{\xi}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{g}}\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}
=δ​𝝃​(t)⋅𝒈\displaystyle=\delta\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\cdot\boldsymbol{g} (D.5)

where δ​𝝃​(0)=𝟎\delta\boldsymbol{\xi}(0)=\boldsymbol{0} is imposed and one can derive 𝝃˙⋅δ​𝒈−δ​𝝃⋅𝒈˙=𝟎\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\cdot\delta\boldsymbol{g}-\delta\boldsymbol{\xi}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{g}}=\boldsymbol{0} with the symmetry property of 𝑱\boldsymbol{J}. It is now clear that under symmetry, the virtual work equates real work. The kinetic energy functional is

Ek​[𝝃​(t)]\displaystyle E_{k}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right] =12​𝝃˙​(t)⋅𝑴​𝝃˙​(t),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)\cdot\boldsymbol{M}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t),
∂tEk​[𝝃⁡(t)]\displaystyle\partial_{t}E_{k}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right] =𝝃˙​(t)⋅𝑴​𝝃¨​(t).\displaystyle=\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)\cdot\boldsymbol{M}\ddot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t). (D.6)

The linear potential energy functional is

Ep​[𝝃​(t)]\displaystyle E_{p}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right] =12​𝝃​(t)⋅𝑲​𝝃​(t),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\cdot\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t),
∂tEp​[𝝃⁡(t)]\displaystyle\partial_{t}E_{p}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right] =𝝃˙​(t)⋅𝑲​𝝃​(t).\displaystyle=\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)\cdot\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t). (D.7)

The overall energy evolution of the system is found to be

𝝃˙​(t)⋅(𝑴​𝝃¨​(t)+𝑪​𝝃˙​(t)+𝑲​𝝃​(t)+𝒈⁡[𝝃⁡(t)])=𝝃˙​(t)⋅𝒇⁡(t)\displaystyle\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)\cdot\left(\boldsymbol{M}\ddot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)+\boldsymbol{C}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)+\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)+\boldsymbol{g}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right]\right)=\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)\cdot\boldsymbol{f}(t)
∂tE=∂tEk+∂tEp+∂tEn​l=𝝃˙​(t)⋅𝒇⁡(t)−𝝃˙​(t)⋅𝑪​𝝃˙​(t)\displaystyle\partial_{t}E=\partial_{t}E_{k}+\partial_{t}E_{p}+\partial_{t}E_{nl}=\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)\cdot\boldsymbol{f}(t)-\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)\cdot\boldsymbol{C}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t) (D.8)

where E⁡[𝝃⁡(t)]=Ek+Ep+En​lE[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)]=E_{k}+E_{p}+E_{nl}.

To apply SAV [29], assume the nonlinear potential energy functional can be rewritten in the square of a scalar variable ψ⁡(t)\psi(t) as

En​l​[𝝃​(t)]\displaystyle E_{nl}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right] =12​ψ​(t)2,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\psi(t)^{2}, (D.9)

where

ψ⁡(t)\displaystyle\psi(t) =2​En​l​[𝝃⁡(t)]+C0,\displaystyle=\sqrt{2}\sqrt{E_{nl}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right]+C_{0}}, (D.10)
ψ˙​(t)\displaystyle\dot{\psi}(t) =12​𝝃˙​(t)⋅𝒈⁡[a⁡(t),𝝃⁡(t),𝝃˙​(t)]En​l​[𝝃⁡(t)]+C0,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)\cdot\boldsymbol{g}\left[a(t),\boldsymbol{\xi}(t),\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)\right]}{\sqrt{E_{nl}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right]+C_{0}}}, (D.11)

and En​l​[𝝃⁡(t)]≥−C0E_{nl}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right]\geq-C_{0} is assumed (bounded from below). Utilizing the Crank–Nicolson scheme described in [30] we have

∫tntn+1𝒈​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n+1}}\boldsymbol{g}\mathrm{d}t =12​∫tntn+1ψ⁡(t)En​l​[𝝃​(t)]​𝒈​[𝝃⁡(t)]​𝑑t\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n+1}}\frac{\psi(t)}{\sqrt{E_{nl}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right]}}\boldsymbol{g}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right]\mathrm{d}t
≈h2​2​ψ⁡(tn)+ψ⁡(tn+1)En​l​[𝝃⁡(tn+12)]+C0​𝒈​[𝝃⁡(tn+12)]\displaystyle\approx\frac{h}{2\sqrt{2}}\frac{\psi(t_{n})+\psi(t_{n+1})}{\sqrt{E_{nl}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+\frac{1}{2}})\right]+C_{0}}}\boldsymbol{g}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+\frac{1}{2}})\right]
≈h2​2​ψ⁡(tn)+ψ⁡(tn+1)En​l​[𝝃⁡(tn)]+h2​E˙n​l​[𝝃⁡(tn)]+C0​𝒈​[𝝃⁡(tn)+h2​𝝃˙​(tn)]\displaystyle\approx\frac{h}{2\sqrt{2}}\frac{\psi(t_{n})+\psi(t_{n+1})}{\sqrt{E_{nl}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})\right]+\frac{h}{2}\dot{E}_{nl}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})\right]+C_{0}}}\boldsymbol{g}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})+\frac{h}{2}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n})\right]
=h2​(ψ⁡(tn)+ψ⁡(tn+1))​𝒔​(𝝃⁡(tn),𝝃˙​(tn)),\displaystyle=\frac{h}{2}\left(\psi(t_{n})+\psi(t_{n+1})\right)\boldsymbol{s}\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n}),\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n})\right), (D.12)

where

𝒔⁡(𝝃⁡(tn),𝝃˙​(tn)):ℝN=𝒈⁡[𝝃⁡(tn)+h2​𝝃˙​(tn)]2​En​l​[𝝃⁡(tn)]+h2​𝝃˙​(tn)⋅𝒈⁡[𝝃⁡(tn)]+C0.\boldsymbol{s}\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n}),\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n})\right):\mathbb{R}^{N}=\frac{\boldsymbol{g}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})+\frac{h}{2}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n})\right]}{\sqrt{2}\sqrt{E_{nl}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})\right]+\frac{h}{2}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n})\cdot\boldsymbol{g}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})\right]+C_{0}}}. (D.13)

Here we encountered the problem of how to approximate the values of 𝒈\boldsymbol{g} and En​lE_{nl} at mid step tn+12t_{n+\frac{1}{2}}. Unlike the several interpolation methods used in [30], we chose a more direct first-order approximation approach using E˙n​l​[𝝃⁡(tn)]\dot{E}_{nl}[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})] and 𝝃˙​(tn)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n}). 𝒈˙​(𝝃​(tn))\dot{\boldsymbol{g}}(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})) was not used because its expression involving 𝑱\boldsymbol{J} may be hard to write, and we instead did a slightly wrose approximation using only 𝝃˙​(tn)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n}); it is also viable to approximate 𝒈˙​(𝝃​(tn))\dot{\boldsymbol{g}}(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})) using 𝒈⁡(𝝃⁡(tn−1))\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n-1})) and 𝒈⁡(𝝃⁡(tn))\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})). Notice that in (D.12) ψ⁡(tn+1)\psi(t_{n+1}) is unknown, so we need to discretize (D.11) for another update scheme

ψ⁡(tn+1)−ψ⁡(tn)\displaystyle\psi(t_{n+1})-\psi(t_{n}) ≈12​(𝝃⁡(tn+1)−𝝃⁡(tn))⋅𝒈⁡(𝝃⁡(tn+12))En​l​[𝝃⁡(tn+12)]\displaystyle\approx\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})\right)\cdot\boldsymbol{g}\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+\frac{1}{2}})\right)}{\sqrt{E_{nl}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+\frac{1}{2}})\right]}}
≈(𝝃⁡(tn+1)−𝝃⁡(tn))⋅𝒔⁡(𝝃⁡(tn),𝝃˙​(tn)).\displaystyle\approx\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})\right)\cdot\boldsymbol{s}\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n}),\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n})\right). (D.14)

It now sufficies to formulate the whole discretization of nonlinear ODEs as

𝑴⁡[𝝃˙​(tn+1)−𝝃˙​(tn)]+𝑪⁡[𝝃⁡(tn+1)−𝝃⁡(tn)]+𝑲​∫tntn+1𝝃​𝑑t+∫tntn+1𝒈⁡[𝝃]​𝑑t=∫tntn+1𝒇​𝑑t\boldsymbol{M}\left[\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n+1})-\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n})\right]+\boldsymbol{C}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})\right]+\boldsymbol{K}\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n+1}}\boldsymbol{\xi}\mathrm{d}t+\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n+1}}\boldsymbol{g}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}\right]\mathrm{d}t=\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n+1}}\boldsymbol{f}\mathrm{d}t (D.15)

Combining this with SAV and

𝝃⁡(tn+1)−𝝃⁡(tn)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n}) ≈h2​[𝝃˙​(tn)+𝝃˙​(tn+1)]\displaystyle\approx\frac{h}{2}\left[\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n})+\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n+1})\right]
𝝃˙​(tn+1)\displaystyle\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n+1}) ≈2h​𝝃​(tn+1)−2h​𝝃​(tn)−𝝃˙​(tn),\displaystyle\approx\frac{2}{h}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\frac{2}{h}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})-\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n}), (D.16)

we obtain the major update scheme:

𝑴⁡[2h​𝝃​(tn+1)−2h​𝝃​(tn)−2​𝝃˙​(tn)]+𝑪⁡[𝝃⁡(tn+1)−𝝃⁡(tn)]+h2​𝑲​[𝝃⁡(tn)+𝝃⁡(tn+1)]\displaystyle\boldsymbol{M}\left[\frac{2}{h}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\frac{2}{h}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})-2\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n})\right]+\boldsymbol{C}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})\right]+\frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{K}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})+\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})\right]
+h​ψ​(tn)​𝒔+h2​𝒔​𝒔⊤​[𝝃⁡(tn+1)−𝝃⁡(tn)]=h​𝒇​(tn)+h22​𝒇˙​(tn)\displaystyle+h\psi(t_{n})\boldsymbol{s}+\frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{s}\boldsymbol{s}^{\top}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})\right]=h\boldsymbol{f}(t_{n})+\frac{h^{2}}{2}\dot{\boldsymbol{f}}(t_{n}) (D.17)
𝝃⁡(tn+1)=𝒁1−1​[𝒁0​𝝃​(tn)+2​𝑴​𝝃˙​(tn)+h​𝒇​(tn)+h22​𝒇˙​(tn)],\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})=\boldsymbol{Z}_{1}^{-1}\left[\boldsymbol{Z}_{0}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})+2\boldsymbol{M}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n})+h\boldsymbol{f}(t_{n})+\frac{h^{2}}{2}\dot{\boldsymbol{f}}(t_{n})\right], (D.18)

where

𝒁0\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Z}_{0} =2h​𝑴+𝑪−h2​𝑲+h2​𝒔​𝒔⊤,\displaystyle=\frac{2}{h}\boldsymbol{M}+\boldsymbol{C}-\frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{K}+\frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{s}\boldsymbol{s}^{\top},
𝒁1\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Z}_{1} =2h​𝑴+𝑪+h2​𝑲+h2​𝒔​𝒔⊤.\displaystyle=\frac{2}{h}\boldsymbol{M}+\boldsymbol{C}+\frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{K}+\frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{s}\boldsymbol{s}^{\top}. (D.19)

Therefore, the SAV update scheme consists of three steps:

  1. 1.

    Input 𝝃⁡(tn)\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n}), 𝝃˙​(tn)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n}), ψ⁡(tn)\psi(t_{n}) into (D.18) to compute 𝝃⁡(tn+1)\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1}).

  2. 2.

    Input 𝝃⁡(tn)\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n}), 𝝃˙​(tn)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n}), 𝝃⁡(tn+1)\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1}) into (D.16) to compute 𝝃˙​(tn+1)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n+1}).

  3. 3.

    Input 𝝃⁡(tn)\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n}), 𝝃˙​(tn)\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n}), 𝝃⁡(tn+1)\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1}), ψ⁡(tn)\psi(t_{n}) into (D.14) to compute ψ⁡(tn+1)\psi(t_{n+1}).

It can be seen that the major update scheme (D.18) is linear w.r.t. 𝝃⁡(tn+1)\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1}), allowing for efficient time stepping. However, we notice that 𝒔​𝒔⊤\boldsymbol{s}\boldsymbol{s}^{\top} in (D.19) is a fully dense N×NN\times N matrix that may be infeasible to store and solve for large number DOFs. This problem can be well alleviated by performing eigen decomposition only once to the time-invariant matrix

𝒁2=2h​𝑴+𝑪+h2​𝑲,𝒁2−1≈𝚽​𝚲​𝚽H,\boldsymbol{Z}_{2}=\frac{2}{h}\boldsymbol{M}+\boldsymbol{C}+\frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{K},\;\boldsymbol{Z}_{2}^{-1}\approx\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\mathrm{H}}, (D.20)

where the dimension of 𝚽\boldsymbol{\Phi} and 𝚲\boldsymbol{\Lambda} is M≪NM\ll N, as only the smallest MM eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors are needed. This should be regarded as a generalized eigenvalue problem because it is desired to avoid explicit matrix inversion. Then by the Shermann–Morrison–Woodbury formula we have

𝒁1−1=(𝒁2+h2​𝒔​𝒔⊤)−1=𝒁2−1−(2h+𝒔⊤​𝒁2−1​𝒔)−1​(𝒁2−1​𝒔)​(𝒁2−1​𝒔)⊤,\boldsymbol{Z}_{1}^{-1}=\left(\boldsymbol{Z}_{2}+\frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{s}\boldsymbol{s}^{\top}\right)^{-1}=\boldsymbol{Z}_{2}^{-1}-\left(\frac{2}{h}+\boldsymbol{s}^{\top}\boldsymbol{Z}_{2}^{-1}\boldsymbol{s}\right)^{-1}\left(\boldsymbol{Z}_{2}^{-1}\boldsymbol{s}\right)\left(\boldsymbol{Z}_{2}^{-1}\boldsymbol{s}\right)^{\top}, (D.21)

where 𝒁2−1\boldsymbol{Z}_{2}^{-1} can be approximated by the truncated eigenvalues and eigenvectors. In this way 𝒁1−1\boldsymbol{Z}_{1}^{-1} multiplying a vector can be efficiently computed without storing and inverting a N×NN\times N dense matrix.

To investigate the energy property of this SAV scheme, we multiply 1h​[𝝃⁡(tn+1)−𝝃⁡(tn)]=12​[𝝃˙​(tn)+𝝃˙​(tn+1)]\frac{1}{h}[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})]=\frac{1}{2}[\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n})+\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n+1})] on both sides of (D.17) to yield1010 10 The reason for the equality 1h​[𝝃⁡(tn+1)−𝝃⁡(tn)]=12​[𝝃˙​(tn)+𝝃˙​(tn+1)]\frac{1}{h}[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})]=\frac{1}{2}[\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n})+\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n+1})] to hold here is that this equation is the actual numerical update scheme we use, no matter how approximate it is to the true continuous values.

12​𝝃˙​(tn+1)⋅𝑴​𝝃˙​(tn+1)−12​𝝃˙​(tn)⋅𝑴​𝝃˙​(tn)+1h​[𝝃⁡(tn+1)−𝝃⁡(tn)]⋅𝑪⁡[𝝃⁡(tn+1)−𝝃⁡(tn)]\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n+1})\cdot\boldsymbol{M}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n+1})-\frac{1}{2}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n})\cdot\boldsymbol{M}\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t_{n})+\frac{1}{h}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})\right]\cdot\boldsymbol{C}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})\right]
+12𝝃(tn+1)⋅𝑲𝝃(tn+1)−12𝝃(tn)⋅𝑲𝝃(tn)+12ψ(tn+1)2−12ψ(tn)2\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})\cdot\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})\cdot\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})+\frac{1}{2}\psi(t_{n+1})^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\psi(t_{n})^{2}
=[𝝃⁡(tn+1)−𝝃⁡(tn)]⋅[𝒇⁡(tn)+h2​𝒇˙​(tn)].\displaystyle=\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})\right]\cdot\left[\boldsymbol{f}(t_{n})+\frac{h}{2}\dot{\boldsymbol{f}}(t_{n})\right]. (D.22)

Combining this with the definition of EE, EkE_{k}, EpE_{p}, En​lE_{nl}, we obtain the evolution of discrete energy as

E⁡[𝝃⁡(tn+1)]−E⁡[𝝃⁡(tn)]=[𝝃⁡(tn+1)−𝝃⁡(tn)]⋅[𝒇⁡(tn)+h2​𝒇˙​(tn)]−1h​‖𝝃⁡(tn+1)−𝝃⁡(tn)‖𝑪2,E\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})\right]-E\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})\right]=\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})\right]\cdot\left[\boldsymbol{f}(t_{n})+\frac{h}{2}\dot{\boldsymbol{f}}(t_{n})\right]-\frac{1}{h}\left\|\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n+1})-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t_{n})\right\|_{\boldsymbol{C}}^{2}, (D.23)

where ‖𝒙‖𝑨2=𝒙⊤​𝑨​𝒙\left\|\boldsymbol{x}\right\|_{\boldsymbol{A}}^{2}=\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}. Since 𝑪\boldsymbol{C} is normally positive definite, the discrete energy is guaranteed to dissipate if 𝒈\boldsymbol{g} is conservative and energy injection through 𝒇⁡(t)\boldsymbol{f}(t) becomes zero. Therefore, it can be concluded that the SAV scheme applied here is energy stable at least for kinetic energy, potential energy, nonlinear “symmetric” energy, and damping.

However, it seems energy stablility may fail to satisfy for the non-symmetric forces 𝒇⁡(t)\boldsymbol{f}(t), which we should actually write as an operator 𝒇⁡[𝝃⁡(t),𝝃˙​(t),𝝃¨​(t)]\boldsymbol{f}[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t),\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t),\ddot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)]. These non-symmetric “endogenous” forces often relate to the coupling between systems. For example, for the soundboard system, 𝒇\boldsymbol{f} is the string’s surface force exerted on the soundboard. If 𝒇\boldsymbol{f} is fully linear with respect to the unknowns, then we can use tn+1t_{n+1} values in 𝒇\boldsymbol{f} to construct linearly implicit schemes which effectively avoids energy unstability, though the formulas may be cumbersome to write. But if 𝒇\boldsymbol{f} exhibits nonlinearity and tn+1t_{n+1} values are used to avoid energy unstability, the scheme would become nonlinearly implicit and it seems only implicit methods, e.g. backward differentiation formula (BDF), can solve for the unknown DOFs. We thus conclude that SAV does not address well the non-symmetric forces, which is vital for modeling the nonlinear coupling between the distinct subsystems of the piano. A tradeoff is to keep using energy-unstabe linear schemes for the nonlinear non-symmetric forces, but perform several iterations as proposed in section 7.2 to compensate. We hope to see more developments regarding efficient and energy-stable schemes for nonlinear inter-system coupling.

We now consider an example of nonlinear potential energy arising from large deformations. For a 3D elastic solid with large deformations, a major source of nonlinearity is the quadratic term in the Green-Lagrange strain. The tensor and vector versions of this nonlinear strain (linear parts omitted) are

ϵn​l​(𝒙,t)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{nl}(\boldsymbol{x},t) =12​∑i=13(∇ui)​(∇ui)⊤,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{3}\left(\nabla u_{i}\right)\left(\nabla u_{i}\right)^{\top}, (D.24)
⇒ϵ→n​l​(𝒙,t)\displaystyle\Rightarrow\overrightarrow{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{nl}(\boldsymbol{x},t) =𝒜⁡(𝒖⁡(𝒙,t))=∑i=13[12​(∂xui)212​(∂yui)212​(∂zui)2(∂xui)​(∂yui)(∂xui)​(∂zui)(∂yui)​(∂zui)]\displaystyle=\mathcal{A}\left(\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x},t)\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\frac{1}{2}\left(\partial_{x}u_{i}\right)^{2}\\ \frac{1}{2}\left(\partial_{y}u_{i}\right)^{2}\\ \frac{1}{2}\left(\partial_{z}u_{i}\right)^{2}\\ \left(\partial_{x}u_{i}\right)\left(\partial_{y}u_{i}\right)\\ \left(\partial_{x}u_{i}\right)\left(\partial_{z}u_{i}\right)\\ \left(\partial_{y}u_{i}\right)\left(\partial_{z}u_{i}\right)\end{array}\right]

where 𝒜:ℝ3→ℝ6\mathcal{A}:\mathbb{R}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{6} is a nonlinear operator. From the nonlinear strain, we find the conservative part of nonlinear strain energy functional as

En​l​[𝒖⁡(𝒙,t)]=12​∫Ω𝒜⁡(𝒖⁡(𝒙,t))⋅𝑫​𝒜​(𝒖⁡(𝒙,t))​𝑑V.E_{nl}\left[\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x},t)\right]=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}\mathcal{A}\left(\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x},t)\right)\cdot\boldsymbol{D}\mathcal{A}\left(\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x},t)\right)\mathrm{d}V. (D.31)

Taking gradient of this functional, the nonlinear stress (body force version) is derived as

∇⋅𝝈n​l=δ​En​l​[𝒖]δ​𝒖.\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{nl}=\frac{\delta E_{nl}\left[\boldsymbol{u}\right]}{\delta\boldsymbol{u}}. (D.32)

Besides EnlE_{\mathrm{nl}}, there may exist damping proportional to the nonlinear stress, leading to the non-conservative part of nonlinear strain energy functional as

En​l​n​c​[𝒖⁡(𝒙,t′),t]=∫0t∫Ω𝒜˙​(𝒖⁡(𝒙,t′))⋅2​μ​𝑫​𝒜˙​(𝒖⁡(𝒙,t′))​𝑑V​d​t′,E_{nlnc}\left[\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x},t^{\prime}),t\right]=\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\Omega}\dot{\mathcal{A}}\left(\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x},t^{\prime})\right)\cdot 2\mu\boldsymbol{D}\dot{\mathcal{A}}\left(\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x},t^{\prime})\right)\mathrm{d}V\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}, (D.33)

where 2​μ2\mu is the viscous damping coefficient. The dynamics of energy dissipation can then be revealed as

∂tEn​l​n​c​[𝒖⁡(𝒙,t′),t]=∫Ω𝒜˙​(𝒖⁡(𝒙,t))⋅2​μ​𝑫​𝒜˙​(𝒖⁡(𝒙,t))​𝑑V.\partial_{t}E_{nlnc}\left[\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x},t^{\prime}),t\right]=\int_{\Omega}\dot{\mathcal{A}}\left(\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x},t)\right)\cdot 2\mu\boldsymbol{D}\dot{\mathcal{A}}\left(\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x},t)\right)\mathrm{d}V. (D.34)

However, consideration of nonlinear damping seems lacking in existing IEQ and SAV research. This may stem from that energy dissipation is path-dependent thus the integration over [0,t][0,t] can not be eliminated. This would require some additional but still acceptable computation costs, and has been covered by our nonlinear energy model D.3. In existing research applying IEQ or SAV to musical instruments simulation, there can be no damping [36] or linear damping [16]. Now we apply space discretization to the nonlinear strain energy functional. Based on (2.15) (2.2) we should be able to find

ϵ→n​l​(𝒙,t)=𝑨⁡(𝒙,𝝃⁡(t))+𝑨0​(𝒙,𝝃⁡(t),𝝃0​(t)),\overrightarrow{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{nl}(\boldsymbol{x},t)=\boldsymbol{A}\left(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right)+\boldsymbol{A}_{0}\left(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\xi}(t),\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0}(t)\right), (D.35)

where 𝑨\boldsymbol{A} and 𝑨0\boldsymbol{A}_{0} are (ℝ3,ℝN)→ℝ6(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{R}^{N})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{6} and (ℝ3,ℝN,ℝN0)→ℝ6(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{R}^{N},\mathbb{R}^{N_{0}})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{6} nonlinear functions (a narrower concept than operator) respectively; 𝑨\boldsymbol{A} accounts for the conservative part and 𝑨0\boldsymbol{A}_{0} accounts for the non-conservative part when 𝝃0\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0} is nonzero. For simplicity, the detailed expression of 𝑨\boldsymbol{A} and 𝑨0\boldsymbol{A}_{0} are currently not presented here. The nonlinear strain energy functional is then

En​l​[𝝃⁡(t)]=12​∫Ω𝑨⁡(𝒙,𝝃⁡(t))⋅𝑫​𝑨​(𝒙,𝝃⁡(t))​𝑑V,E_{nl}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right]=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}\boldsymbol{A}\left(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right)\cdot\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{A}\left(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right)\mathrm{d}V, (D.36)

and its variation and first derivative are

δ​En​l​[𝝃⁡(t)]\displaystyle\delta E_{nl}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right] =δ​𝝃⋅𝑩⁡(𝝃⁡(t)),\displaystyle=\delta\boldsymbol{\xi}\cdot\boldsymbol{B}\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right),
∂tEn​l​[𝝃⁡(t)]\displaystyle\partial_{t}E_{nl}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right] =𝝃˙​(t)⋅𝑩​(𝝃​(t)),\displaystyle=\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)\cdot\boldsymbol{B}\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right),
𝑩⁡(𝝃)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{B}\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\right) =∫Ω[∇𝝃𝑨​(𝒙,𝝃)]⊤​𝑫​𝑨​(𝒙,𝝃)​𝑑V\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\left[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\boldsymbol{A}\left(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\xi}\right)\right]^{\top}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{A}\left(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\xi}\right)\mathrm{d}V (D.37)

Since 𝑨0\boldsymbol{A}_{0} relates to 𝝃0​(t)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0}(t), i.e. nonzero Dirichlet boundary conditions, it does not satisfy the symmetry (self-adjoint) condition previously highlighted. We thereby seek to compute the nonlinear virtual strain energy as

δ​En​l,0​[𝝃⁡(t)]\displaystyle\delta E_{nl,0}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\right] =δ​𝝃⋅𝑩0​(𝝃⁡(t),𝝃0​(t))\displaystyle=\delta\boldsymbol{\xi}\cdot\boldsymbol{B}_{0}\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t),\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0}(t)\right)
𝑩0​(𝝃,𝝃0)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{B}_{0}\left(\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0}\right) =∫Ω[∇𝝃𝑨​(𝒙,𝝃)]⊤​𝑫​𝑨0​(𝒙,𝝃,𝝃0)​𝑑V\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\left[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\boldsymbol{A}\left(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\xi}\right)\right]^{\top}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{A}_{0}\left(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0}\right)\mathrm{d}V
+∫Ω[∇𝝃𝑨0(𝒙,𝝃,𝝃0)]⊤𝑫[𝑨(𝒙,𝝃)+𝑨0(𝒙,𝝃,𝝃0)]dV\displaystyle+\int_{\Omega}\left[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\boldsymbol{A}_{0}\left(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0}\right)\right]^{\top}\boldsymbol{D}\left[\boldsymbol{A}\left(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\xi}\right)+\boldsymbol{A}_{0}\left(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0}\right)\right]\mathrm{d}V (D.38)

Finally, we add 𝑩\boldsymbol{B} to 𝒈\boldsymbol{g} and add −𝑩0-\boldsymbol{B}_{0} to 𝒇\boldsymbol{f} in the nonlinear ODEs (D.1). Note that since the nonlinear stress belongs to conservative forces, its corresponding nonlinear strain energy functional (D.36) has eliminated the integration over [0,t][0,t].
